sentence: Two sounds count as separate phonemes in a language only if swapping one for the other can change a word's meaning. English keeps the contrast between the voiced and voiceless dental fricatives because the difference between thigh and thy rides entirely on that single feature. Where no such minimal pair can be constructed, the sounds are merely allophones, predictable variants conditioned by their phonetic surroundings.

The aspirated and unaspirated stops of English never distinguish words, so a speaker hears the puff of air on the p of pin and the absence of it on the p of spin as the same sound. In Hindi, by contrast, that puff is contrastive: the aspirated and unaspirated bilabial stops produce entirely different lexical items, which forces analysts to assign them to separate phonemes.

A minimal pair isolates a single point of contrast while holding everything else constant. The words bat and pat differ only in the voicing of the initial consonant, and that lone difference is enough to confirm that the two stops belong to distinct phonemes. When analysts cannot find such a pair, they sometimes settle for a near-minimal pair, where the surrounding context is identical enough to rule out conditioning effects.

Vowel systems lend themselves to dense webs of minimal pairs. Beat, bit, bait, bet, bat, but, bought, and boat all share the same consonantal frame, so each contrast among them isolates a vowel quality. The size of such a set gives a rough measure of how crowded a language's vowel space is and how finely listeners must discriminate formant patterns.

Complementary distribution is the diagnostic that demotes two sounds to allophones of one phoneme. The clear and dark variants of the English lateral never appear in the same environment: one surfaces before vowels, the other after them. Because no context admits both, no minimal pair can exist, and the analyst concludes that a single underlying unit is realized differently according to position.

Tone languages multiply the opportunities for minimal contrast. In Mandarin a single syllable shape can carry four distinct pitch contours, each yielding a separate word, so the syllable ma alone furnishes a four-way set distinguished by tone and nothing else. Analysts treat the contours as suprasegmental phonemes precisely because they pass the substitution test.

Phonemic status is language-specific rather than universal. The velar nasal is a full phoneme in English, where sin and sing form a minimal pair, but in many languages it occurs only as a positional variant of an alveolar nasal before velar stops. The same physical articulation thus plays a contrastive role in one system and a purely predictable one in another.

Functional load measures how much work a given contrast does across the lexicon. The distinction between the two English th sounds carries a famously light load, supported by only a handful of minimal pairs, whereas the voicing contrast in stops underpins thousands. Contrasts with low functional load are the ones most likely to collapse through historical merger.

Neutralization occurs when a contrast that holds in most positions is suspended in a particular environment. German obstruents lose their voicing distinction word-finally, so the underlying difference between the stems of Rad and Rat surfaces only when a vowel-initial suffix follows. In the bare form the minimal pair collapses, and the listener must rely on grammatical context to recover the intended word.

Length can be contrastive in its own right. Finnish distinguishes short and long vowels, and also short and long consonants, so that pairs like tuli, tuuli, and tulli differ only in the duration of one segment. Such systems show that the timing of an articulation, not merely its quality, can serve as the sole carrier of lexical meaning.

Languages distribute meaning across word forms in strikingly different proportions. Isolating languages such as Mandarin keep morphemes as separate free-standing words, so a sentence is a sequence of monomorphemic units. Synthetic languages instead pack several grammatical meanings into a single word, and the extreme polysynthetic case bundles what English would express as a whole clause into one heavily affixed verb.

Agglutinating languages string affixes together like beads, each morpheme contributing one discrete piece of meaning and remaining easy to segment. A Turkish verb may carry separate, identifiable suffixes for tense, person, number, and negation, and a competent analyst can slice the word at clean boundaries. The transparency of the joints is what defines the type.

Fusional languages blur the boundaries that agglutinating ones keep crisp. A single Latin verb ending simultaneously signals tense, mood, person, and number, and no scalpel can separate those meanings into individual morphs. The portmanteau character of such endings is the hallmark of fusion, where one form does the work of several distinct grammatical categories.

The index of synthesis counts morphemes per word, and the index of fusion measures how cleanly those morphemes can be separated. The two scales are independent: a language can be highly synthetic yet agglutinating, packing many transparent affixes into a word, or only mildly synthetic yet strongly fusional, with a few opaque portmanteau endings doing concentrated grammatical work.

Polysynthetic languages can incorporate nouns directly into the verb, so that the object becomes a morpheme inside the predicate rather than a separate word. A single verb in such a language may translate as an entire English sentence, complete with subject, object, and several adverbial notions, all expressed by a chain of affixes and incorporated roots.

No language is purely one type. English is broadly analytic, relying on word order and separate function words, yet it retains fusional remnants in irregular verbs where tense and aspect are signaled by an internal vowel change rather than a separable suffix. Typological labels name dominant tendencies, not absolute categories.

Root-and-pattern morphology, characteristic of Semitic languages, interleaves a consonantal root with a vowel template. The root carries the core semantic field while the surrounding pattern of vowels and prosodic shape signals the grammatical category. A single triliteral root can thus generate dozens of related words by being poured into different templatic molds.

Templatic and concatenative morphology differ in how a form is built. Concatenative systems add affixes in a linear chain before or after a stable stem. Templatic systems instead distribute material discontinuously, so that the morphemes are not arranged in sequence but woven through one another, and segmentation requires identifying tiers rather than slicing a string.

Suppletion is the limiting case of irregularity, where a morphological relationship holds between forms that share no phonological material at all. The English comparative of good is better, and the past tense of go is went, pairs that the grammar treats as inflectionally related even though no rule could derive one shape from the other.

Reduplication copies all or part of a stem to signal a grammatical meaning. Some languages mark the plural by doubling the first syllable of the noun, others express intensity or repeated action by reduplicating the verb. The copied material is a genuine morpheme even though it has no fixed phonological content of its own, taking its shape from whatever base it attaches to.

A constituent is a group of words that the grammar treats as a single unit, and several diagnostics reveal its boundaries. If a string can be moved to the front of the clause as a block, it is probably a constituent. The phrase to the old bookshop in the corner can be fronted whole, which shows that its words cohere syntactically rather than merely sitting side by side.

Substitution by a pro-form is a classic constituency test. If a sequence of words can be replaced by a single pronoun, a form like it, there, or do so, then that sequence behaves as one syntactic object. The fact that the whole verb phrase can be replaced by do so shows that the verb and its complements form a unit excluding the subject.

The coordination test relies on the principle that only like constituents may be joined by a conjunction. If two strings can be coordinated and yield a grammatical result, they are likely constituents of the same category. When a sequence cannot enter into coordination with an obvious phrase of a given type, the analyst has evidence that it does not form a unit at all.

The cleft test embeds a candidate string in the focus position of an it-cleft. If the result is grammatical, the string is a constituent. The sentence shape it was the old map that she found places whatever fills the focus slot under scrutiny, and only genuine constituents can occupy that position without producing an ill-formed clause.

Constituency tests do not always agree, and their conflicts are themselves informative. A string may pass the movement test but fail the substitution test, suggesting that constituency is not a single uniform notion. Some analysts respond by positing different structures at different levels of representation, while others treat the tests as probing distinct grammatical relations.

The answer-fragment test exploits the fact that a stand-alone reply to a question must be a constituent. When the response to a query is a bare phrase rather than a full clause, that phrase must be a syntactic unit, since elliptical answers cannot consist of arbitrary word strings that lack internal cohesion.

Ellipsis provides another window onto structure. Verb-phrase ellipsis deletes a stretch of material under identity with an antecedent, and only a constituent can be elided in this way. If a sequence can go missing while leaving behind a grammatical sentence interpreted as containing it, the elided string must have been a coherent unit.

The constituency of strings is often ambiguous, and a single sentence can support more than one bracketing. The phrase old men and women admits two structures depending on whether the adjective scopes over the conjunction or only over its first conjunct. Each bracketing predicts different test results, and the divergence is exactly what makes the sentence structurally ambiguous.

Adjuncts and complements differ in their structural attachment, and constituency tests can tease them apart. A complement combines tightly with the verb, while an adjunct attaches higher and more loosely. The do-so substitution test distinguishes them, since the pro-form can strand an adjunct outside it but cannot leave a complement behind.

Tree diagrams encode the results of constituency tests as hierarchical structure. Each node groups the words dominated beneath it into a unit, and the branching geometry predicts which strings should pass which diagnostics. A well-supported tree is one whose constituents are independently confirmed by movement, substitution, coordination, and clefting working in concert.

Case is a grammatical category that marks a noun phrase for its relation to the verb or to other elements in the clause. A nominative form signals the subject, an accusative the direct object, and a dative typically the recipient. Languages with rich case morphology can afford freer word order, since the endings rather than position carry the relational information.

The genitive case canonically encodes possession and broader associative relations between two nouns. Beyond ownership it can mark the material something is made of, the whole of which something is a part, or the agent of a nominalized action. Its semantic breadth makes the genitive one of the most polyfunctional cases in the typical case inventory.

Locative cases situate an entity in space, and many languages split this domain finely. Separate cases may distinguish location at a place, motion toward it, and motion away from it, and some systems add a further contrast between being inside, on top of, and adjacent to a landmark. The verb need not specify direction when the case ending already encodes it.

Case syncretism occurs when distinct grammatical relations share a single morphological form. A language may use one ending for both the nominative and the accusative of neuter nouns, leaving the listener to recover the intended role from word order or agreement. Syncretism reveals that the abstract case categories and their surface exponents are not in one-to-one correspondence.

Structural cases are assigned by the grammar according to syntactic position, while inherent or lexical cases are demanded by a particular verb regardless of position. A verb may idiosyncratically require its object in the dative even though an ordinary transitive verb would take an accusative. The distinction matters because structural case can change under passivization while inherent case typically does not.

Case inventories vary enormously in size. English has all but lost nominal case, preserving it only in the pronouns, where a residual contrast between he and him survives. Finnish, at the other extreme, distinguishes well over a dozen cases, many of them spatial, so that what English expresses with prepositions Finnish folds into the noun itself.

The vocative case marks a noun used to address someone directly, standing apart from the clause's argument structure. It does not name a participant in the event described but rather identifies the person being spoken to. Some languages give the vocative a distinct ending; others reuse the nominative form, signaling the function purely through intonation and position.

Differential object marking means that not every object receives overt case. Many languages mark an object morphologically only when it is high in animacy or definiteness, leaving inanimate or indefinite objects unmarked. The pattern shows that case assignment can be sensitive to semantic properties of the noun phrase rather than to syntactic role alone.

Case stacking, found in some Australian languages, allows a noun to bear more than one case suffix at once. An inner case may register the noun's relation within a phrase while an outer case registers the relation of the whole phrase to the clause. The layered morphology makes the noun a record of nested grammatical dependencies.

The instrumental case marks the means by which an action is carried out, the tool or substance employed. It frequently extends to mark the comitative notion of accompaniment, since the entity one acts with and the entity one acts by means of are conceptually adjacent. Tracking such extensions across languages reveals recurring paths of semantic generalization.

The comparative method reconstructs an unattested ancestor language by systematically comparing its descendants. The analyst assembles cognate sets, words in related languages that descend from a common original, and looks for recurrent correspondences among their sounds. Where the same correspondence appears again and again, it can be projected back as a single proto-sound.

Regular sound correspondences are the backbone of the comparative method. If a particular consonant in one language consistently matches a different consonant in a sister language across many words, the match cannot be coincidence. The regularity itself is the evidence, since chance resemblances do not recur systematically through the lexicon.

Reconstructed forms are marked with an asterisk to signal that they are inferred rather than attested. A starred proto-form is a hypothesis about the shape of an ancestor word, justified by the daughter forms it must have produced. The asterisk is a constant reminder that the comparative method yields models, not recovered documents.

Borrowed words can masquerade as cognates and must be filtered out before reconstruction proceeds. A loanword shares form and meaning across languages not because of common inheritance but because of contact. Analysts detect loans by their failure to obey the regular sound correspondences that genuine cognates display, since borrowed material often enters after the relevant sound changes have run.

The method assumes that sound change is regular, applying to every word that meets its phonetic conditions. Without this assumption the recurrent correspondences would have no explanation. Apparent exceptions are then either borrowings, analogical reformations, or instances of a further sound change whose conditioning environment must itself be discovered.

Internal reconstruction complements the comparative method by inferring an earlier stage from the irregularities within a single language. Alternations that look arbitrary in the present grammar may be residues of a once-regular process. By undoing the later change, the analyst recovers a more uniform earlier system without needing any sister language for comparison.

Shared innovations, not shared retentions, are what subgroup languages within a family. Two languages may both preserve an archaic feature simply because neither lost it, which proves nothing about their closeness. But if they share a peculiar change that the rest of the family did not undergo, that common innovation points to a period of exclusive common descent.

The reconstructed proto-language is a system, not a list of words, and the comparative method aims to recover its phonology, morphology, and even aspects of its syntax. A plausible reconstruction must be typologically natural, resembling the kinds of systems attested in living languages, since an ancestor that violated universal tendencies would itself need explaining.

Directionality matters in reconstruction because some sound changes are far more common than their reverses. A stop becoming a fricative is well attested, while the opposite path is rare. When the daughter languages disagree, the analyst favors the proto-form from which the attested forms could most naturally have evolved, using the typology of sound change as a guide.

The discovery of systematic correspondences among Sanskrit, Greek, and Latin in the late eighteenth century launched the comparative method as a discipline. The recognition that such resemblances were too pervasive to be accidental, and too regular to be borrowing, implied a lost common source. From that inference grew the entire enterprise of reconstructing language families.

A conversational implicature is something a speaker conveys without literally saying it, recoverable by reasoning about why those particular words were chosen. When a reference letter praises only a candidate's punctuality, the reader infers a low assessment of more relevant qualities. Nothing negative was stated, yet the cooperative assumption forces the unflattering conclusion.

Scalar implicature arises from terms that sit on a scale of informativeness. Saying that some of the guests arrived implicates that not all of them did, because a speaker who knew all had arrived would have said so. The stronger term was available and rejected, and the listener treats that rejection as meaningful.

Implicatures are cancellable, which distinguishes them from logical entailments. A speaker can say that some guests arrived and then add that in fact all of them did, without contradiction. The follow-up suspends the usual inference, showing that the implicature was a defeasible pragmatic enrichment rather than part of the sentence's literal content.

The cooperative principle holds that participants in a conversation tacitly agree to contribute appropriately to the shared purpose of the exchange. From this overarching principle flow more specific expectations governing how much to say, how truthful to be, how relevant to remain, and how clearly to express oneself. Implicatures are generated when a speaker appears to flout one of these expectations while still being cooperative.

Flouting a maxim openly, rather than quietly violating it, triggers a search for a deeper meaning. An obviously false statement uttered in plain view of its falsity cannot be a lie, so the listener reinterprets it as irony or hyperbole. The blatant breach signals that the literal content is not the intended message.

Conventional implicatures differ from conversational ones in being tied to particular words rather than to general reasoning. The word but contributes a sense of contrast that does not affect truth conditions and cannot be cancelled. This contrastive meaning rides along with the lexical item itself, independent of the conversational context.

Relevance is a powerful engine of inference. When a reply seems off-topic, the listener assumes it is nonetheless relevant and constructs the bridging assumptions needed to make it so. An answer about the weather to a question about going out is understood as a refusal, because only that interpretation restores the relevance the speaker is presumed to maintain.

Generalized implicatures arise by default in almost any context, while particularized ones depend on the specific situation. The inference from some to not all is generalized, attaching to the word almost wherever it appears. An inference that a particular utterance constitutes a polite refusal is particularized, holding only given the surrounding circumstances of that exchange.

Implicature reasoning can be iterated. A speaker may anticipate what a listener will infer and exploit that anticipation, and a sophisticated listener may in turn reason about the speaker's anticipation. This recursive mind-reading underlies subtle phenomena such as faint praise, where the strategic choice of a weak compliment is calculated to produce a negative inference.

Presupposition is a distinct kind of pragmatic content, information treated as already taken for granted rather than newly asserted. A question about whether someone has stopped a habit presupposes that the habit existed. Unlike an implicature, a presupposition survives under negation and questioning, which is the standard diagnostic for telling the two apart.

Languages are grouped into families on the basis of shared descent from a common ancestor. Membership in a family is a genealogical claim, asserting that the languages diverged through ordinary transmission across generations. The claim is supported by the same kind of systematic correspondences that the comparative method uses to reconstruct the proto-language.

A language isolate is a language with no demonstrable relatives, a family of one. Basque is the standard European example, resisting every attempt to link it convincingly to a larger group. An isolate is not a language without a history but one whose relatives, if they ever existed, have left no traceable descendants.

Family trees branch into ever finer subgroups, each defined by a set of shared innovations. The Indo-European family splits into branches such as Germanic, Romance, Slavic, and Indo-Iranian, and each branch subdivides further. The tree model captures successive splits but cannot easily represent later convergence between separated branches.

The wave model supplements the tree by depicting innovations spreading outward across a dialect continuum like ripples on water. Features radiate from centers of innovation and weaken with distance, so neighboring varieties share traits regardless of strict descent. Where the tree shows clean splits, the wave model shows overlapping, gradient diffusion.

Proposed deep relationships, such as macro-families uniting several established families under one ancestor, remain controversial. As the time depth increases, the regular correspondences grow faint, since accumulated sound change erodes the cognate material. Beyond a certain age the signal of common descent sinks below the noise of chance resemblance.

Genealogical classification must be kept separate from typological classification. Two unrelated languages can share a structural type, such as verb-final word order, simply by parallel development or contact. Belonging to the same type says nothing about belonging to the same family, since type is a synchronic property and family is a historical relationship.

Some of the world's largest families contain hundreds of languages spread over vast territory. Austronesian stretches across an enormous expanse of the Pacific and Indian oceans, and Niger-Congo encompasses much of sub-Saharan Africa. The internal structure of such giant families is itself a major research program, with many subgroups still under debate.

Lexicostatistics attempts to estimate the degree of relationship between languages by counting how many items of a basic vocabulary list they share as cognates. The method is fast but blunt, since it treats all vocabulary alike and can be misled by borrowing. Most historical linguists regard it as a rough heuristic rather than a substitute for the rigorous comparative method.

A proto-language is the reconstructed common ancestor at the root of a family tree, and intermediate proto-languages can be reconstructed at the root of each subgroup. The full classification is thus a nested set of reconstructions, with the proto-language of a branch standing as a daughter of the family's overall proto-language.

Unclassified languages exist where documentation is too sparse to support any genealogical claim. A language known only from a short word list collected before it fell silent may show tantalizing resemblances to neighbors, but without enough data the correspondences cannot be tested. Such languages remain in a provisional limbo, neither isolates nor confirmed members of any family.

Deictic expressions are words whose reference shifts with the situation of utterance. The pronoun I picks out whoever is speaking, the word here designates wherever the speaker is, and now anchors to the moment of speech. Such words cannot be interpreted from the sentence alone; the listener must locate the speech event in order to fix what they denote.

Spatial deixis encodes distance from a reference point, usually the speaker. A two-term system contrasts a proximal demonstrative with a distal one, this against that. Some languages add a third term oriented toward the addressee, distinguishing what is near me, near you, and near neither of us, giving the deictic field an explicitly interpersonal geometry.

Temporal deixis locates events relative to the moment of speaking. Tense itself is deictic, since past and future are defined by their relation to now. Adverbs like yesterday and tomorrow are equally anchored, and a recorded message that says I will return tomorrow becomes indeterminate once detached from the day on which it was produced.

Person deixis grammaticalizes the roles of the speech situation. First person identifies the speaker, second person the addressee, and third person whoever is neither. Many languages elaborate this core with distinctions of number and with an inclusive-exclusive contrast that specifies whether the addressee is counted among the group denoted by we.

Discourse deixis points not at the world but at the unfolding text itself. Expressions like in the previous paragraph or as I will argue below refer to portions of the discourse. They orient the reader within the structure of the message, treating the text as a space through which speaker and listener move together.

Social deixis encodes the relationship between participants in the speech event. Honorific pronouns and respectful verb forms register the relative status or familiarity of speaker and addressee. The choice between a formal and an informal second-person pronoun is not about who is being addressed but about how the speaker positions the social distance between them.

The deictic center is the default origin from which deictic expressions are calculated, normally the speaker, the place of speaking, and the time of speaking. Narrative can shift this center, projecting it onto a character so that here and now track the character's vantage rather than the narrator's. Such projection is what gives free indirect discourse its distinctive doubled perspective.

Gestural and symbolic uses of deictics differ in how reference is fixed. A gestural use of that requires the listener to monitor an accompanying pointing gesture or gaze. A symbolic use needs only general knowledge of the situation, as when this city is understood without any gesture because the location of the utterance already supplies the referent.

Indexicality is the broader semiotic property of which deixis is the linguistic case: a sign is indexical when it points to something by virtue of a real connection to it rather than by resemblance or convention. Smoke indexes fire, and the word here indexes the speaker's location. Deictic words are the lexicalized, grammaticalized members of this larger indexical family.

Deictic projection can fail and produce ambiguity. A note left on a door reading back in an hour leaves the reader unable to compute the intended return time, because the now to which the hour is added is the moment of writing, not the moment of reading. The breakdown shows how thoroughly deictic interpretation depends on access to the original speech situation.

The sense of a word is its place in a network of relations to other words, while its reference is what it picks out in the world. Two expressions can share a referent yet differ in sense, as the morning star and the evening star both denote one planet but present it under different descriptions. Lexical semantics studies the sense side of this divide.

Hyponymy is the relation of inclusion between word meanings. The meaning of robin is included in the meaning of bird, so every robin is a bird but not conversely. Such relations chain into taxonomies, with each level a hyponym of the one above it, building the lexicon into a hierarchy of progressively more general categories.

Antonymy is not a single relation but several. Gradable antonyms like hot and cold admit intermediate degrees and comparison. Complementary antonyms like dead and alive partition a domain with no middle ground. Converse antonyms like buy and sell describe the same situation from opposite participant perspectives. Each subtype behaves differently under negation.

Polysemy is the property of a single word having multiple related senses, while homonymy involves distinct words that happen to share a form. The word mouth has related senses for the body part and the opening of a river, a case of polysemy. The two words spelled bank are homonyms, their meanings connected by no semantic thread.

Componential analysis decomposes word meanings into bundles of semantic features. Within a kinship vocabulary, terms can be distinguished by features of sex, generation, and lineality, so that the difference between two terms reduces to a difference in one feature value. The approach treats the lexicon as built from a small inventory of recurring meaning components.

Prototype theory challenges the idea that category membership is all-or-nothing. Speakers judge some members of a category as better examples than others, treating a robin as a more central bird than a penguin. Word meanings, on this view, are organized around prototypical instances, with membership graded by similarity to the prototype rather than fixed by a checklist of necessary features.

Semantic fields group words that carve up a single conceptual domain. The vocabulary of cooking, of color, or of motion forms such a field, and the meaning of any one term is shaped by the others that border it. A word's content is partly negative, defined by what neighboring words leave for it to cover.

Meronymy is the part-whole relation among word meanings, as finger is a meronym of hand and hand of arm. Unlike hyponymy, meronymy is not always transitive across several steps, since a feature true of a part need not transfer cleanly to the part of a part. The relation interacts subtly with how speakers reason about wholes and their components.

Selectional restrictions are the constraints a word places on the meanings of the words it combines with. The verb drink requires a liquid as its object, and pairing it with a solid produces semantic anomaly even when the syntax is impeccable. Such restrictions show that lexical meaning constrains combination, not merely category-level grammar.

Vagueness and ambiguity are distinct ways a word can fail to fix a single interpretation. An ambiguous word has several discrete meanings, and context selects one. A vague word has a single meaning whose boundaries are fuzzy, so that the word tall offers no sharp threshold. Tests involving conjunction reduction can tell the two apart, since they behave differently under elliptical coordination.

In a tone language, pitch is lexical: a change in the pitch contour of a syllable can change the word, just as a change in a consonant would. The pitch is part of the word's phonological identity, stored in the lexicon alongside its consonants and vowels. Most languages of this kind are concentrated in particular regions, but the type recurs across unrelated families.

Register tone systems contrast level pitch heights, distinguishing words by whether a syllable is high, mid, or low. Contour tone systems instead contrast moving pitches, rising and falling glides treated as unitary tonal categories. Some languages combine both, layering contour distinctions on top of register ones.

Tone is not always anchored rigidly to a syllable. In many languages tones behave as autonomous units that can shift, spread, or float free of their original host. A tone may detach from a deleted syllable and dock onto a neighbor, evidence that tone occupies a separate tier from the segments it eventually associates with.

Intonation, unlike lexical tone, operates over whole phrases and conveys meaning at the level of the utterance rather than the word. A rising contour at the end of a clause can turn a declarative string into a question, and the placement of a pitch accent can signal which element the speaker treats as new or contrastive.

Pitch accent systems occupy a middle ground between tone and stress. In such a system each word has at most one accented syllable, and the accent is realized as a distinctive pitch movement rather than mere loudness. The accent's location is contrastive, but the system lacks the dense tonal specification of a full tone language.

Downdrift is the gradual lowering of pitch over the course of an utterance, so that a high tone late in a sentence may be physically lower than a low tone near its start. Listeners normalize for this drift, judging tone relative to its local neighbors rather than against an absolute pitch scale. The phenomenon shows that tonal categories are perceived comparatively.

Tone sandhi refers to the systematic ways tones change in connected speech. A tone may shift its shape depending on the tones that precede or follow it, so that a syllable's citation tone is not the tone it surfaces with in a phrase. The alternations are rule-governed and form a substantial part of a tone language's phonology.

Intonational phrasing chunks an utterance into units, each with its own pitch pattern. The boundaries between these units are marked by pitch movements and often by lengthening of the final syllable. The way a speaker phrases a sentence can disambiguate its structure, signaling to the listener how the words are grouped.

The autosegmental representation of tone separates a tonal tier from a segmental tier and links the two with association lines. This architecture explains why one tone can spread across several syllables and why several tones can crowd onto one. Tone behaves as a thing in its own right, with its own combinatorial possibilities, rather than as a mere property of vowels.

Languages without lexical tone still use pitch heavily, but they confine it to the phrasal level. English deploys intonation to mark questions, focus, and the speaker's attitude, and to signal whether a list is complete. The same acoustic dimension thus carries word-level information in one type of language and only utterance-level information in another.

Alignment describes how a language groups the core arguments of its clauses. A nominative-accusative system treats the single argument of an intransitive verb like the agent of a transitive one, marking both alike and reserving a distinct form for the patient. The grouping reflects a decision to align the lone intransitive argument with the actor.

An ergative-absolutive system makes the opposite choice. It treats the single argument of an intransitive verb like the patient of a transitive one, giving both the absolutive form, and singles out the transitive agent with a special ergative marking. The lone intransitive argument is thus aligned with the undergoer rather than the actor.

Many ergative languages are not consistently ergative throughout their grammar. A language may show ergative marking on nouns but accusative patterning in its verbal agreement, a mismatch known as split alignment. The split shows that alignment is a property of particular grammatical subsystems rather than of a language as an undivided whole.

Split ergativity is often conditioned by tense or aspect. A language may pattern ergatively in the perfective and accusatively in the imperfective, so the same verb takes different argument marking depending on its aspectual form. The recurrence of this particular split across unrelated languages suggests a deep connection between aspect and alignment.

The animacy hierarchy can also govern an ergative split. Pronouns and animate nouns may follow accusative marking while inanimate nouns follow ergative marking, with the boundary falling at a predictable point on the scale. High-animacy arguments are the prototypical agents, and the grammar treats them accordingly.

Syntactic ergativity goes beyond morphology and shows up in how clauses combine. In a syntactically ergative language, processes such as relativization may target the absolutive argument freely but block the transitive agent, requiring a special construction to relativize on it. Morphological ergativity, by contrast, leaves the syntax fundamentally accusative.

The antipassive construction is to ergative languages roughly what the passive is to accusative ones. It demotes or removes the patient and recasts the clause so that the agent appears in the absolutive case. The construction is the typical resource for placing the agent into the privileged syntactic role when ergative patterning would otherwise block it.

Active-stative alignment offers a third pattern. The single argument of an intransitive verb is marked according to its semantic role: agentive arguments pattern with transitive agents, while patientive arguments pattern with transitive patients. The intransitive subject is split in two, sorted by whether it acts or undergoes.

Tripartite alignment marks all three core argument types distinctly, giving separate forms to the transitive agent, the transitive patient, and the intransitive subject. The system is rare because it is the least economical, using three markers where the more common patterns make do with two. Its rarity is itself a typological fact in need of explanation.

Alignment is most visible in case marking but also surfaces in verb agreement and word order. A language can be ergative in one of these domains and accusative in another, and the term alignment names the abstract grouping pattern that each domain instantiates. Comparing the domains within a single language reveals how loosely the subsystems are coordinated.

A pidgin is a simplified contact language that arises when speakers of mutually unintelligible tongues need a common medium for limited communication. It has no native speakers, a restricted vocabulary, and a pared-down grammar shaped by the practical needs of trade or labor. A pidgin is a second language for everyone who uses it.

A creole emerges when a pidgin acquires a community of native speakers and, in becoming someone's first language, expands into a full linguistic system. The grammar gains the complexity needed to express anything a natural language must express. The transition from pidgin to creole is the transition from an auxiliary code to a mother tongue.

Creole vocabulary typically derives overwhelmingly from one language, the lexifier, while the grammar resembles that lexifier far less closely. This mismatch between where the words come from and where the structure comes from is one of the central puzzles of creole studies, and competing theories explain it by appeal to substrate influence, universal tendencies, or the dynamics of restricted input.

The substrate hypothesis holds that the grammatical structure of a creole is largely inherited from the native languages of the people who created it. Speakers carried over the patterns of their first languages and recast the lexifier's vocabulary into those familiar molds. On this account a creole's grammar is a mosaic of its substrate ancestors.

The language bioprogram hypothesis argues instead that children creating a creole draw on an innate grammatical blueprint when the pidgin input they receive is too impoverished to supply a full grammar. The structural similarities observed among creoles of different ancestries are taken as evidence that the same inborn default settings are surfacing.

Decreolization describes the process by which a creole, under continued contact with its lexifier, gradually shifts its grammar toward that prestige language. The result is a continuum of varieties ranging from the conservative basilect through intermediate mesolects to an acrolect close to the standard. Speakers may command a stretch of this continuum and shift along it according to situation.

Pidgins themselves can stabilize and elaborate without ever acquiring native speakers. An extended pidgin develops a wider vocabulary and a more articulated grammar because it comes to serve a broad range of communicative functions. Such a pidgin blurs the neat boundary with creoles, since structural complexity can grow even in the absence of nativization.

Many creoles share recurrent grammatical features regardless of which languages contributed to them. They tend to express tense, mood, and aspect through separate preverbal particles rather than through inflection, and to mark plurality with a free word rather than a suffix. Whether these similarities reflect common origins, common substrates, or universal pressures remains debated.

The status of creoles as ordinary natural languages is now firmly established, against an older view that treated them as broken or deficient versions of their lexifiers. A creole has a systematic phonology, a productive morphology, and a complex syntax, and it serves all the functions any first language serves. Its origin in contact does not make it linguistically lesser.

Mixed languages differ from creoles in their genesis. Where a creole arises from a pidgin under conditions of disrupted transmission, a mixed language typically combines the grammar of one source with the vocabulary of another in a community that already speaks both. The split is cleaner, often along the line between structure and lexicon, and the social setting is one of bilingualism rather than pidgin contact.

Displacement occurs when an element is pronounced in one position but interpreted as belonging to another. In a question, the questioned phrase appears at the front of the clause yet is understood as the object of a verb deep inside it. Syntacticians model this mismatch as movement, an operation that relocates the element while leaving a trace at its original site.

Wh-movement fronts an interrogative phrase to the edge of the clause. The gap it leaves behind is the position where the phrase receives its grammatical role, and the relation between the fronted phrase and the gap is the dependency the analysis must capture. Some languages leave the interrogative phrase in place instead, an option that itself needs explaining.

Island constraints limit how far displacement can reach. Certain syntactic configurations are islands, structures out of which no element may be extracted. A phrase trapped inside a relative clause or a coordinate structure cannot be questioned from outside it, and the resulting ungrammaticality reveals the boundaries that movement may not cross.

Long-distance dependencies can span several clauses. A questioned phrase may be fronted from inside a deeply embedded complement, and the dependency between it and its gap stretches across every intervening clause boundary. Analyses that posit successive-cyclic movement break the long dependency into a chain of shorter, locally constrained steps.

Raising constructions move a noun phrase out of a lower clause into the subject position of a higher one. The raised phrase satisfies a grammatical requirement of the upper clause while still being understood as an argument of the lower verb. The verb in the upper clause assigns it no semantic role, which is the diagnostic that distinguishes raising from superficially similar control structures.

Passive constructions can be analyzed as movement of the underlying object into subject position. The patient, normally realized after the verb, surfaces before it, and the agent is either suppressed or expressed in an oblique phrase. The reordering changes which argument occupies the prominent grammatical role without changing the event the sentence describes.

Topicalization moves a phrase to the front of the clause to mark it as the topic, the thing the sentence is about. Unlike question formation it produces a declarative, and the fronted element is often set off prosodically. The construction shows that displacement serves discourse-organizational ends, not only the formation of questions.

Traces are the silent residue that movement leaves at the launching site. Though unpronounced, a trace is held to be syntactically real, occupying the position from which the moved element draws its interpretation. Evidence for traces comes from indirect effects, such as the way an apparently distant phrase can still control agreement or block other operations from its original location.

Scrambling is a freer kind of displacement found in languages with flexible word order. Arguments and adjuncts can be reordered within the clause to suit discourse needs, producing several surface orders with the same basic meaning. Whether scrambling is the same operation as the more constrained movements of question formation is a long-standing question.

The crossover phenomenon shows that movement interacts with pronoun interpretation. When a phrase moves over a pronoun that would otherwise be construed as referring to it, the coreference reading can become unavailable. The pattern is taken as evidence that the trace left by movement participates in the same binding relations as an ordinary noun phrase.

When speakers of different languages interact regularly, features pass from one language into the other, a process called borrowing. The most easily borrowed material is vocabulary, especially words for new objects and concepts. A borrowed word is typically reshaped to fit the sound system of the receiving language, so that it loses sounds the borrower's phonology cannot accommodate.

A loanword can be adopted whole, or its meaning can be borrowed while its form is freshly built from native material. The second strategy yields a calque, a word-by-word translation of a foreign expression. A calque looks native because every morpheme is, yet its internal structure betrays a foreign model that the speakers chose to imitate rather than import.

Borrowing is not confined to vocabulary. Under intense and prolonged contact, languages can borrow sounds, morphological patterns, and even syntactic structures. Structural borrowing is slower and harder than lexical borrowing, and its presence signals a deep, sustained contact relationship rather than a casual exchange of words.

A linguistic area, or sprachbund, is a region where unrelated or distantly related languages have come to share structural features through long contact. The shared traits cut across family boundaries, so they cannot be explained by common descent. The convergence is instead the cumulative residue of centuries of multilingual interaction within a single geographic zone.

The distinction between borrowing and shift-induced interference depends on who is doing the changing. Borrowing happens when a community imports features into its own well-maintained language. Interference happens when speakers shifting to a new language carry features of their old one into it. The two processes affect different parts of the grammar and leave different signatures.

Some loanwords are so thoroughly assimilated that ordinary speakers no longer sense their foreign origin. Centuries of use erase the marks of importation, and the word obeys every native rule of inflection and derivation. Only the historical linguist, tracing sound correspondences, can recover that the word once entered from another language.

A borrowing hierarchy ranks grammatical material by how readily it is borrowed. Content words go first, then function words, then bound morphology, with the most tightly integrated structure resisting longest. The hierarchy is a probabilistic generalization rather than an absolute law, but its broad shape recurs across many documented contact situations.

Loanword adaptation reveals the phonology of the borrowing language by showing how it copes with foreign sounds and structures. A consonant cluster the receiving language forbids may be broken up by an inserted vowel, and a foreign vowel may be replaced by the nearest native equivalent. The repairs are systematic, exposing the constraints that govern native words too.

The direction and intensity of borrowing often track social asymmetries between communities. A language associated with prestige, administration, or commerce tends to supply more words than it receives. The vocabulary of a language can thus serve as a stratified record of past contacts, with successive layers of loans deposited by successive periods of outside influence.

Phonetic transcription aims to represent speech sounds independently of the inconsistencies of ordinary spelling. The International Phonetic Alphabet provides one symbol for each distinctive sound, so that the same symbol always denotes the same articulation regardless of which language is being written. The goal is a notation in which writing and pronunciation never diverge.

Consonant symbols in the alphabet are organized by place of articulation, manner of articulation, and voicing. The chart arranges places from the lips back to the glottis along one axis and manners from full closure to open approximation along the other. Reading off a cell of the chart yields a precise articulatory description of the sound it represents.

Vowels are plotted on a quadrilateral whose axes correspond to the height of the tongue and how far forward it sits. A vowel's position on this chart captures its quality, and rounding of the lips is noted as a further dimension. The geometry of the chart mirrors the geometry of the vocal tract during vowel production.

Diacritics extend the alphabet by modifying a base symbol to record fine phonetic detail. A small mark can indicate that a sound is nasalized, that a vowel is slightly raised, or that a consonant is articulated with a particular secondary gesture. The diacritics allow a transcription to be as precise as the analyst's ear and purpose require.

A broad transcription records only the phonemic contrasts of a language, ignoring predictable detail. A narrow transcription adds the allophonic variation and the diacritics needed to capture how the sounds are actually realized. The choice of breadth depends on the analytic question, since a broad transcription answers what is contrastive and a narrow one answers what is pronounced.

Square brackets and slashes mark the two levels of transcription. A string enclosed in slashes is a phonemic representation, abstracting away from predictable variation. A string in square brackets is a phonetic representation, claiming to record the actual sounds. The bracketing is not decoration but a statement about the kind of object being transcribed.

Suprasegmental features such as stress, length, and tone have their own symbols and marks. A raised vertical line before a syllable indicates primary stress, a colon-like symbol marks length, and accent marks of various shapes notate tones. These notations sit alongside the segmental symbols to capture properties that span more than a single sound.

The alphabet is designed to be extensible, since fieldwork constantly turns up sounds not yet catalogued. New symbols and diacritics have been added over the alphabet's history as the inventory of attested human speech sounds grew. The notation is thus a living standard, revised as the documentation of the world's languages advances.

Some categories of sound are unusually demanding to transcribe. Clicks, implosives, and ejectives involve airstream mechanisms other than the ordinary outflow of lung air, and the alphabet provides dedicated symbols for them. Transcribing such sounds requires the analyst to attend not only to where and how a closure is made but also to where the moving air comes from.

Transcription is an interpretive act, not a mechanical recording. Two trained phoneticians may transcribe the same utterance slightly differently, because deciding which category a borderline sound falls into involves judgment. The alphabet supplies a shared vocabulary, but using it well demands a trained ear and an explicit awareness of the choices being made.

Code-switching is the alternation between two languages within a single conversation, and often within a single sentence. Far from being a sign of confusion or deficiency, it is a skilled performance that requires fluent command of both grammars. A speaker who switches mid-clause must coordinate two systems simultaneously without violating the rules of either.

Intersentential switching occurs at sentence boundaries, with one language used for one sentence and the other for the next. Intrasentential switching occurs within a sentence, with the boundary falling at a clause edge or even between a verb and its object. The two patterns make different demands on the bilingual's processing.

Code-switching is not random but constrained. Switches tend to occur at points where the grammars of the two languages are compatible, and certain junctures resist switching altogether. Researchers have proposed grammatical constraints to predict where a switch can and cannot fall, treating the bilingual's mixed output as a rule-governed system in its own right.

One influential model identifies a matrix language that supplies the grammatical frame of a mixed clause and an embedded language that contributes inserted material. The matrix language provides the function words and the morphological structure, while the embedded language supplies content items slotted into that structure. The asymmetry gives the mixed utterance a backbone.

Switching carries social meaning beyond the referential content of the words. A speaker may switch to signal group identity, to mark a shift in topic or tone, to quote someone, or to include or exclude a bystander. The choice of language at each moment is a resource for managing the social texture of the interaction.

Code-switching is distinguished from borrowing by its scale and integration. A borrowed word becomes a permanent part of the receiving language's lexicon and is used even by monolinguals. A switched stretch of the other language is a momentary, on-the-fly use that does not enter the lexicon and presupposes bilingual competence in both speaker and addressee.

The equivalence constraint predicts that switches occur where the surface word orders of the two languages coincide. Where the languages would order the same elements differently, a switch at that point would force a violation of one grammar, so speakers avoid it. The constraint treats the mixed sentence as bound by both rule systems at once.

Some bilingual communities develop such dense and habitual switching that the alternation becomes the unmarked, ordinary mode of speaking. In these settings switching no longer carries a special signal each time it occurs, since it is the default. The mixed code itself becomes a marker of community identity, used as a unified style rather than as a series of pointed moves.

Even single inserted words pose an analytic puzzle: a lone item from the other language might be a momentary switch or a nonce borrowing. The two categories shade into one another, and deciding between them requires looking at how morphologically integrated the item is and whether the surrounding community treats it as established. The boundary is gradient rather than sharp.

A phonological rule states how an underlying form is converted into its surface pronunciation. The rule specifies a class of sounds, a change they undergo, and the environment that triggers the change. Such rules capture the systematic adjustments that turn the abstract representation stored in the lexicon into the concrete sequence a speaker actually produces.

Assimilation is the process by which a sound becomes more similar to a neighbor. A nasal consonant commonly takes on the place of articulation of a following stop, so that the nasal in a prefix shifts to match whatever consonant begins the stem. The change reduces the articulatory effort of moving between adjacent sounds.

Dissimilation works in the opposite direction, making two nearby sounds less alike. When a word contains two similar sounds close together, one of them may change to break the resemblance. Dissimilation is rarer than assimilation and is often sporadic rather than fully regular, affecting some words and sparing others.

Epenthesis inserts a sound that is not present in the underlying form, typically to repair an illicit structure. A vowel may be inserted to break up a consonant cluster the language forbids, or a consonant may be inserted between two vowels. The inserted segment exists only to satisfy the language's constraints on permissible sequences.

Deletion removes a sound that the underlying form contains. A vowel in an unstressed syllable may drop, or a consonant may be lost at a word edge or within a cluster. Deletion and epenthesis are mirror processes, one subtracting and one adding, and both serve to bring forms into line with what the language's structure permits.

Rules can be ordered so that the output of one rule feeds the input of another. When the first rule creates the environment that the second rule needs, the relationship is called feeding. When the first rule instead destroys an environment the second would have used, the relationship is bleeding. Rule ordering is needed to derive the correct surface forms.

Lenition weakens a consonant, moving it along a path from a strong articulation toward a weaker one. A stop may become a fricative, a fricative an approximant, and ultimately the consonant may vanish entirely. Lenition characteristically targets consonants in weak positions, such as between vowels, where articulatory pressure to reduce effort is greatest.

Optimality theory replaces ordered rules with ranked constraints. Instead of deriving a surface form step by step, the grammar generates many candidate outputs and selects the one that best satisfies a hierarchy of conflicting constraints. The winning candidate is the one whose violations fall on the lowest-ranked constraints, since higher-ranked constraints take absolute priority.

Some phonological alternations are productive, applying automatically to new words including borrowings and invented forms. Others are merely lexicalized residues, frozen patterns that survive in particular words but no longer generalize. Testing a process against nonce words shows whether it is a live rule of the synchronic grammar or a fossil of an earlier stage.

Convergence under contact can make two languages grow grammatically alike while their vocabularies stay distinct. Long bilingualism lets speakers gradually align the structures of one language with the other, so that translation becomes nearly word-for-word. The lexicons remain separate badges of identity even as the underlying grammars quietly merge.

Triggering is the observation that an item shared or similar across both languages can prompt a switch in the words that follow it. A proper name or a cognate sits at the junction of the two systems, and once the speaker has uttered it the conversation may continue in the other language. The shared item acts as a hinge between codes.

Underlying representations are abstract because a single morpheme may surface in several shapes depending on its environment. The analyst posits one stored form and a set of rules that derive each variant. The underlying form is chosen so that the rules needed to produce every surface alternant are as simple and general as possible.

Thematic roles classify the participants in an event by the part they play. An agent initiates and controls the action, a patient undergoes a change of state, an instrument is the means employed, and an experiencer registers a mental or perceptual state. These roles describe semantic relations that hold no matter how the sentence is grammatically arranged.

The argument structure of a verb is the specification of how many participants it requires and what roles they bear. An intransitive verb licenses one argument, a transitive verb two, and a ditransitive verb three. The verb's lexical entry must record these requirements, since a clause that fails to supply the demanded arguments is ungrammatical.

Linking rules govern how thematic roles map onto grammatical relations. The agent role typically surfaces as the subject and the patient as the object, but the correspondence is not automatic. Passive and other constructions rearrange the mapping, so that a patient can become the subject while the agent is demoted or omitted.

Some verbs alternate in their argument realization. The verb break can appear with both an agent and a patient, or with the patient alone, the latter use describing the change of state without naming a cause. The alternation shows that a single verb can project more than one argument structure, with regular relationships between the variants.

A theme is the entity that moves or is located, distinct from a patient that undergoes a change. The recipient of a transfer and the goal of a motion are further roles, and the source role names where something comes from. Fine-grained role inventories try to capture exactly which semantic distinctions the grammar is sensitive to.

Argument structure interacts with case and agreement. The argument bearing the agent role often controls verb agreement and receives a particular case, and which argument does so reveals the language's alignment. Tracking how roles, cases, and agreement line up exposes the architecture connecting meaning to grammatical form.

The theta criterion holds that each argument bears exactly one thematic role and each role is assigned to exactly one argument. The principle rules out a noun phrase that would receive two roles and a role that goes unassigned. It enforces a tidy one-to-one match between the semantic participants of an event and the grammatical arguments of the clause.

Causative constructions add an argument, introducing a causer who brings about the event described by the base verb. A non-causative clause with one participant becomes a causative clause with two, the new participant standing outside the original event as its instigator. Languages build causatives by affixation, by separate verbs, or by lexical pairs.

Applicative constructions promote an oblique participant to the status of a core object. A beneficiary or a location, normally expressed in a peripheral phrase, is raised into the central argument structure of the clause and the verb is marked accordingly. The construction reshapes which semantic roles count as core arguments.

Unaccusative and unergative verbs are both intransitive but differ in the role of their single argument. The lone argument of an unergative verb is agent-like, an actor, while that of an unaccusative verb is patient-like, an undergoer. Although both verb types take one argument, the grammar treats the two classes differently in several constructions.

Word frequencies in any large body of text are spectacularly uneven. A handful of words account for an enormous share of all tokens, while the great majority of word types occur only a few times each. The most frequent word in an English corpus alone may cover several percent of every running text.

Zipf's law states a regularity in this unevenness: the frequency of a word is roughly inversely proportional to its rank in a frequency list. The second-ranked word occurs about half as often as the first, the third about a third as often, and so on. Plotted on logarithmic axes, the relationship traces a nearly straight line.

The vocabulary of a corpus divides into a small set of very frequent function words and a vast tail of rare content words. The function words at the top of the list are grammatical glue, while the long tail contains specific nouns, verbs, and adjectives that each appear only sparingly. Most word types are rare and most word tokens are common.

The number of distinct word types in a corpus keeps growing as more text is added, never reaching a ceiling. Each new stretch of text introduces fresh rare words, so the type count rises steadily even when the token count is already enormous. This unbounded growth of vocabulary is a basic property of natural language samples.

A hapax legomenon is a word that occurs exactly once in a given corpus. Such words are surprisingly numerous, often making up a large fraction of all the word types present. Their abundance is a direct consequence of the heavily skewed frequency distribution that governs how words are spread through text.

Frequency interacts with word length. The most frequent words tend to be short, and the long tail of rare words tends to contain longer forms. The pattern is often interpreted as a pressure toward efficiency, with the items used most often being kept brief to reduce the cumulative effort of communication.

Frequency shapes how words behave in the grammar over time. High-frequency words resist regularizing pressure and preserve irregular forms, which is why the most common verbs of a language are so often the irregular ones. Rare words, lacking this protection, are pulled toward the regular pattern.

The skewed frequency distribution has practical consequences for anyone sampling language. A modest corpus captures the common words well but represents the rare ones poorly or not at all. Reliable evidence about infrequent words demands disproportionately large amounts of text, because each rare word contributes so few occurrences.

Frequency effects pervade language processing. Frequent words are recognized faster and produced more readily than rare ones of the same length and structure. The frequency with which a speaker has encountered a word leaves a measurable trace in how quickly and easily it can later be accessed.

The frequency profile of a text or speaker can serve as a kind of fingerprint. The relative rates at which function words appear are stable and largely unconscious, and they vary enough between authors to support statistical attribution. Quantitative study of word frequency thus connects the structure of the lexicon to questions of style and identity.

Agreement is the grammatical phenomenon whereby one word varies its form to match a property of another. A verb may change its ending to reflect the person and number of its subject, so that the subject and the verb are said to agree. The matching is obligatory, and a mismatch produces an ungrammatical sentence.

The element whose features are copied is the controller of agreement, and the element that varies to reflect them is the target. A subject noun phrase typically controls and a verb typically targets, but adjectives, determiners, and other elements can act as targets too. The controller-target distinction organizes the analysis of any agreement system.

Agreement can register a range of features: person, number, gender, and sometimes case or definiteness. Which features a language tracks in agreement is itself a typological variable. Some languages copy only number onto the verb, others copy person and number and gender all at once.

Gender concord requires modifiers to match the grammatical gender of their head noun. An adjective, an article, and a participle may all take endings that signal the gender class of the noun they depend on. The repeated marking knits the noun phrase together by spreading a single feature across all its parts.

Long-distance agreement holds between elements separated by clause boundaries. A verb in one clause may agree with an argument inside an embedded clause, copying features across a syntactic gap. Such cases are theoretically important because they test how far an agreement relation can reach.

Agreement can be controlled by semantic properties rather than strict grammatical form. A collective noun grammatically singular may take a plural verb when the speaker construes it as a set of individuals. This semantic agreement, sometimes called agreement according to sense, shows that the controller's meaning, not only its form, can drive the target.

When a verb has more than one potential controller, languages differ in which one wins. Agreement with the nearer of two conjoined subjects, called attraction, is one common resolution. The patterns of resolution under competing controllers reveal the underlying mechanism that selects the source of agreement features.

Default agreement appears when no suitable controller is available. An impersonal construction with no referential subject still requires the verb to carry some ending, and the language supplies a default value, often third person singular. The default fills the slot that the agreement system insists on filling.

Agreement morphology can make overt pronouns unnecessary. In a language where the verb's ending fully identifies the person and number of the subject, the subject pronoun may be freely omitted. Such pro-drop languages let rich verbal agreement carry the information that a separate pronoun would otherwise supply.

Polypersonal agreement marks more than one argument on the verb. A single verb form may simultaneously cross-reference its subject and its object, and sometimes an indirect object as well. The verb thereby becomes a compact record of the entire argument configuration of its clause.

Phonotactics is the set of constraints governing which sequences of sounds a language permits. Every language allows some combinations and forbids others, and a string of sounds can be perfectly pronounceable yet still be ill-formed because it violates these constraints. The constraints are part of a speaker's tacit knowledge.

The syllable is the basic unit over which phonotactic constraints are stated. It divides into an onset, the consonants before the vowel, a nucleus, usually the vowel itself, and a coda, the consonants after it. The nucleus and coda together form the rime, the part relevant to rhyme.

Languages differ in how elaborate their syllables may be. Some permit only a consonant followed by a vowel, the simplest possible shape. Others allow heavy clusters in both onset and coda, so that a single syllable can contain a long string of consonants flanking the vowel.

The sonority sequencing principle constrains the internal shape of the syllable. Sonority should rise from the onset toward the nucleus and fall again toward the coda. Clusters that respect this rising-then-falling profile are favored, and those that violate it are cross-linguistically rare or repaired.

A speaker's phonotactic knowledge extends to words never heard before. Presented with an invented form, a speaker can judge whether it is a possible word of the language even though it is not an actual one. This ability to rate nonce words shows that phonotactics is a generative system, not a list of attested strings.

Loanwords are reshaped to obey the phonotactics of the borrowing language. A consonant cluster the borrower forbids may be broken up by an inserted vowel, and a forbidden coda may be deleted or repaired. The systematic adjustments expose the constraints by showing what the language refuses to tolerate.

Syllable weight distinguishes light syllables from heavy ones, and the distinction matters for stress and meter. A syllable with a long vowel or a coda consonant typically counts as heavy, while a short open syllable counts as light. Many stress systems are sensitive to this weight, attracting stress to heavy syllables.

The maximal onset principle holds that, when a consonant could in principle belong to either of two adjacent syllables, it is assigned to the onset of the later syllable rather than the coda of the earlier one. The principle reflects a cross-linguistic preference for onsets and a disfavoring of codas.

Some languages permit syllabic consonants, segments that serve as the nucleus of a syllable in place of a vowel. A nasal or a liquid can carry the syllable, bearing its stress and weight. Such cases show that the nucleus position is defined functionally, by its role in the syllable, not strictly by vowel-hood.

Phonotactic constraints can be probabilistic rather than absolute. Some sequences are not forbidden outright but merely rare, and speakers are sensitive to these gradient differences. A word built from low-probability but legal sequences is judged less word-like than one built from high-probability sequences.

Long before producing words, infants pass through stages of vocal development. Cooing gives way to canonical babbling, in which the child produces repeated consonant-vowel syllables. The sounds of babbling gradually drift toward the inventory of the surrounding language, so that the babble of children in different communities begins to diverge.

The first recognizable words typically appear around the end of the first year. Early vocabulary grows slowly at first, then in many children accelerates sharply in a period of rapid expansion. The words of this stage tend to name salient objects, people, and routines in the child's immediate world.

The one-word stage is followed by a two-word stage in which the child combines items into simple ordered pairs. These early combinations already respect word order and express recognizable relations such as possession, location, and action. Grammatical function words and inflections are largely absent.

Early child speech is often described as telegraphic because it omits the small grammatical words and endings while keeping the content words. The child says the bare nouns and verbs that carry the message and leaves out articles, auxiliaries, and inflectional suffixes, much as a telegram once stripped a sentence to its essentials.

Children pass through a stage of overregularization, applying a regular grammatical pattern to forms that are in fact irregular. A child who once said an irregular past tense correctly may later produce a regularized version, having extracted the general rule. The error is evidence that the child has internalized a productive rule rather than memorized each form.

Acquisition proceeds in a broadly consistent order across children learning the same language. Certain grammatical morphemes are mastered early and others late, and the sequence is fairly stable even though the pace varies. The regularity of the order suggests that acquisition is constrained, not a free response to whatever input happens to arrive.

Children's comprehension typically runs ahead of their production. A child may understand a grammatical construction reliably before being able to produce it, so that what the child says underestimates what the child knows. Measuring acquisition therefore requires probing comprehension as well as recording speech.

The input children receive is often addressed to them in a special register, with simplified vocabulary, shorter sentences, and exaggerated intonation. Whether this child-directed speech is necessary for acquisition is debated, since children in some communities hear little of it yet still acquire their language fully.

Children acquire the grammar of their language without explicit instruction and despite input that is finite and imperfect. They generalize beyond the sentences they have heard, producing and understanding novel ones. This gap between the limited evidence and the rich knowledge attained is the central puzzle that theories of acquisition try to solve.

By around the age of four or five, a child has acquired the core grammar of the native language, controlling its sound system, its inflectional morphology, and its basic sentence structures. Refinements of vocabulary, of complex syntax, and of discourse skill continue for years, but the foundational system is in place remarkably early.

Word meanings drift over time, and the study of these shifts is semantic change. A word that once denoted one concept may come to denote a related but distinct one, and the path of change can often be reconstructed from earlier records. The meaning a word carries today is a snapshot of an ongoing process.

Broadening, or generalization, occurs when a word extends its meaning to cover a wider range of referents. A term that once named a specific item may come to name a whole category. The word's range expands, so that what it can be applied to grows more inclusive than it once was.

Narrowing is the opposite process, in which a word's meaning contracts to cover a smaller range than before. A general term becomes specialized, restricted to a particular subtype of what it formerly denoted. The word survives but its scope of application shrinks.

Amelioration is a shift in which a word acquires a more positive connotation over time. A term that once carried a neutral or negative sense comes to be used approvingly. The change is not in what the word denotes so much as in the evaluative coloring attached to it.

Pejoration is the reverse, a slide toward a more negative connotation. A word that once was neutral or even favorable comes to carry disapproval or contempt. Many words that now insult began as ordinary descriptions, their hostile sense accumulated through the company they kept.

Metaphorical extension drives much semantic change. A word for a concrete object or a bodily part is applied to an abstract domain on the basis of a perceived similarity. The mouth of a river and the foot of a mountain are extensions in which a body-part term has been carried into the language of landscape.

Metonymy extends a word's meaning by association rather than resemblance. A word for one thing comes to denote something contiguous to it, a container standing for its contents or a place standing for an institution. The new sense is reached by a step along a real-world connection rather than an analogy.

Semantic bleaching is the loss of specific content as a word grammaticalizes. A full lexical item with a rich meaning gradually empties out, retaining only an abstract grammatical function. The original concrete sense fades while the word becomes a marker of tense, aspect, or some other category.
