Semantic change is usually gradual, proceeding through a stage in which old and new senses coexist. For a time the word is polysemous, and context selects which sense is intended. Only later may one sense crowd out the other, leaving the change complete and the earlier meaning recoverable only from old texts.

Euphemism is a recurrent source of semantic change. A mild word adopted to avoid a harsh one may itself absorb the harshness it was meant to soften, and so be replaced in turn. The cycle, in which each polite substitute is eventually contaminated, drives a steady turnover of vocabulary in sensitive domains.

Distinctive feature theory holds that speech sounds are not atomic but are composed of smaller properties. A sound is a bundle of features, each specifying one articulatory or acoustic dimension. Two sounds differ by differing in the value of one or more of these features rather than by being wholly unrelated wholes.

Features are typically binary, taking a plus or a minus value. A sound is either voiced or voiceless, either nasal or oral, and the grammar refers to these values directly. The binary format lets a phonological rule pick out exactly the class of sounds that share a given feature value.

Natural classes are sets of sounds that share one or more features, and phonological rules apply to natural classes rather than to arbitrary lists. A rule that affects all voiced stops is natural because the targeted sounds share features. A rule targeting an unmotivated assortment of unrelated sounds would not be expected to exist.

Features capture why certain sounds pattern together. The sounds that trigger a particular alternation, or that undergo it, usually form a natural class, and the feature description states the property they have in common. The feature inventory is justified by its success in picking out exactly the groupings that the grammars of the world's languages refer to.

Place features specify where in the vocal tract a constriction is formed. Labial, coronal, and dorsal are major place categories, and finer features locate the constriction more precisely. A change of place, such as a nasal taking on the place of a following stop, is a change in these features.

Manner features specify how the airstream is modified. The contrast between a complete closure and a narrow channel that produces friction is a manner contrast, as is the contrast between a stop and a sound made with the nasal passage open. Manner features distinguish the broad categories of consonant articulation.

Some features are privative rather than binary, present or simply absent rather than plus or minus. A privative feature characterizes the sounds that have a property but says nothing positive about the sounds that lack it. Whether a given feature should be treated as binary or privative is an empirical question.

Features are organized into a hierarchical structure rather than an unordered list. Feature geometry groups related features under shared nodes, so that a rule can spread or delete a whole group at once. The geometry predicts which features tend to act together in phonological processes.

Underspecification theory holds that not every feature value is present in the underlying representation. Predictable values are left unspecified and filled in by rule, so the stored form contains only the information that the grammar cannot otherwise supply. The approach tries to keep lexical representations as economical as possible.

Features mediate between phonology and phonetics. They are abstract enough to enter into grammatical rules and concrete enough to be grounded in articulation and acoustics. This double character is what lets feature theory connect the categorical patterns of the sound system to the continuous physical signal of speech.

Speech act theory holds that to say something is, very often, to do something. An utterance is not merely a description of the world but an action performed through language. Promising, ordering, apologizing, and naming are all things accomplished by speaking, and the theory studies what makes such acts succeed.

A single utterance can be analyzed on three levels. The locutionary act is the act of producing a meaningful sentence. The illocutionary act is what the speaker does in saying it, such as warning or requesting. The perlocutionary act is the effect the utterance has on the hearer, such as frightening or persuading.

Performative utterances are statements that, in being uttered, perform the very act they name. To say the words of a promise under the right conditions is to promise, not to report a promising. Such utterances are neither true nor false; instead they succeed or fail, are felicitous or infelicitous.

Felicity conditions are the circumstances that must hold for a speech act to come off. A promise requires that the speaker intends and is able to do the promised thing, that the act has not already been done, and that the hearer wants it done. When these conditions fail, the act misfires rather than being false.

Illocutionary acts can be sorted into broad classes by what they do. Some commit the speaker to the truth of a proposition, some attempt to get the hearer to act, some commit the speaker to a future course of action, some express a psychological state, and some change the world by being declared. The classification organizes the space of things language can do.

An indirect speech act is one performed by way of another. A speaker who asks whether the hearer can pass the salt is literally posing a question about ability but is understood as making a request. The hearer recovers the intended act by reasoning past the literal force of the words.

The success of an indirect speech act depends on shared inferential routines. Both speaker and hearer rely on conventions and on the cooperative assumption that the literal interpretation, being pointless in context, is not the intended one. The indirect act is computed, not decoded from a fixed code.

Declarations are the speech acts that most strikingly change the world. Pronouncing a verdict, naming a ship, or opening a meeting alters the social reality simply by being said by the right person in the right setting. The institutional context supplies the authority that makes the words effective.

Speech act theory bears on the analysis of meaning because it shows that the literal content of a sentence underdetermines what is done with it. The same sentence can be a statement, a warning, or a threat depending on the act it is used to perform. A full account of communication must include the force of an utterance alongside its content.

The notion of uptake captures the hearer's role in completing an illocutionary act. For certain acts to count as performed, the hearer must recognize the speaker's communicative intention. The act is not a private exercise of the speaker but a social transaction that requires the hearer's understanding to be fully realized.

Dialectology studies the geographic variation of language, mapping how features differ from place to place. It treats the territory over which a language is spoken not as uniform but as a patchwork of local varieties. The discipline records which forms are used where and seeks the patterns in their distribution.

An isogloss is a line drawn on a map separating the area where one linguistic feature is used from the area where a competing feature is used. On one side speakers say one word or use one pronunciation, and on the other they use the alternative. The isogloss makes a single point of variation visible as a boundary.

Isoglosses for different features rarely coincide exactly. Each feature has its own boundary, and the lines crisscross the map rather than stacking neatly. The lack of coincidence shows that dialects are not sharply bounded objects but bundles of independently varying traits.

Where several isoglosses do run close together, they form a bundle, and a dense bundle marks a major dialect division. The thicker the bundle, the more features change at once as one crosses it, and the more salient the boundary feels to speakers. Bundles are how dialectology identifies the principal dialect areas.

A dialect continuum is a chain of varieties in which each is mutually intelligible with its neighbors but the varieties at the far ends are not. There is no sharp break anywhere along the chain, only gradual cumulative difference. The continuum shows that the line between dialect and language can be a matter of degree.

Traditional dialect surveys collected data by interviewing older rural speakers, often asking for the local words for everyday objects and activities. The resulting answers were plotted on maps to reveal the geography of variation. The choice of conservative speakers aimed to capture the regional forms before they were leveled.

A relic area is a region where an older form survives after it has been replaced elsewhere. Such areas are often peripheral or isolated, less exposed to the spread of innovations. Mapping relic areas helps reconstruct the earlier state of the language from which the present distribution descended.

The transition zone between two dialect areas contains mixed and intermediate forms. Speakers there may use forms from both sides or hybrids of them, and the isoglosses for individual features are spread out rather than concentrated. The breadth of the transition zone measures how gradual the shift between the dialects is.

Linguistic innovations spread across the map in patterns that dialectology can trace. A new form may radiate outward from a population center, reaching nearby places before distant ones, or it may jump from one city to another and only later fill in the countryside between. The shape of the spread is itself a finding.

Perceptual dialectology shifts the focus from the distribution of features to the beliefs of ordinary speakers about that distribution. It asks where non-linguists think the dialect boundaries lie and what attitudes they attach to each region's speech. The mental map of dialects can differ instructively from the map drawn by isoglosses.

Tense locates a situation in time relative to the moment of speaking. A past tense places the situation before that moment, a future tense after it, and a present tense at or around it. Tense is deictic, since its reference point is the act of utterance itself.

Aspect concerns the internal temporal shape of a situation rather than its location in time. The perfective views a situation as a complete whole, while the imperfective views it from within, as ongoing or unfolding. The same event can be presented either way, and the choice of aspect reflects how the speaker construes it.

Tense and aspect are distinct dimensions that can combine freely. A situation can be located in the past and viewed perfectively, located in the past and viewed imperfectively, and so on. Languages package these two dimensions differently, some marking each separately and some fusing them in a single form.

The progressive aspect presents a situation as in progress at a reference time, focusing on its ongoing middle and leaving its endpoints out of view. It contrasts with a simple form that may present the situation as a bounded whole. The progressive thus zooms in on the interior of an event.

The perfect relates a situation to a later reference time, marking its current relevance or its resulting state. It is not simply a past tense, since it does not merely locate an event earlier but connects it to the present moment. The perfect occupies a space between tense and aspect.

Modality concerns the speaker's stance toward the factuality of a situation, expressing possibility, necessity, obligation, or permission. A modal does not assert that something is the case but qualifies it, marking it as required, allowed, or merely possible. Modality opens the clause onto alternatives to the actual world.

Epistemic modality expresses the speaker's degree of certainty about a proposition, while deontic modality expresses obligation and permission. The same modal word can often be read either way, so that a sentence about what someone must do may concern either a logical inference or a requirement. Context selects the intended flavor.

Evidentiality, grammaticalized in many languages, marks the source of the speaker's information. A verb form may signal whether the speaker witnessed the event, inferred it, or learned of it by hearsay. Where evidentials are obligatory, every statement carries an explicit indication of how its content was come by.

Mood is the grammatical category through which modality is often expressed in the verb. An indicative mood presents a situation as factual, while subjunctive, conditional, and other moods present it as hypothetical, desired, or contingent. The mood of the verb signals how the clause's content is to be taken.

The interaction of tense, aspect, and modality produces a rich system for situating and qualifying events. A single verb form in a richly inflected language can simultaneously locate a situation in time, characterize its temporal contour, and mark the speaker's commitment to it. Disentangling these layered meanings is a central task of grammatical analysis.

Grammaticalization is the process by which lexical words turn into grammatical markers, and grammatical markers turn into still more abstract ones. A noun or a verb with full referential meaning gradually loses that meaning and takes on a structural function. The word for a body part may end up as a preposition, and a verb of motion may end up as a future marker.

Grammaticalization pathways are strikingly similar across unrelated languages. A verb meaning to go very often becomes a marker of future tense, and a verb meaning to finish very often becomes a marker of completed aspect. The recurrence of these particular routes suggests that grammaticalization follows channels carved by general cognitive tendencies.

As a word grammaticalizes it typically undergoes phonetic reduction. Losing stress and shortening, the form may fuse with a neighboring word and end up as an affix. The erosion of phonological substance accompanies the loss of semantic substance, the two kinds of bleaching proceeding together.

Grammaticalization is generally unidirectional. The change runs from lexical to grammatical and from less grammatical to more grammatical, and the reverse path is rare. A grammatical marker seldom regains the full lexical meaning it once had, which is why the cline is treated as having a built-in direction.

An intermediate stage of grammaticalization shows the source word and the grammaticalized form coexisting. The lexical verb and the auxiliary derived from it may both remain in use, distinguished by context. This layering of older and newer functions is a hallmark of a change in progress.

Semantic bleaching in grammaticalization is the gradual loss of concrete content. The future marker derived from a verb of motion no longer carries any sense of physical movement, retaining only the abstract notion of futurity. What is left is a thin grammatical meaning stripped of its lexical origin.

Grammaticalization often proceeds through metaphorical extension, with a concrete spatial meaning recruited to express an abstract temporal or logical one. The mapping from space to time is especially productive, so that words for location and direction become words for tense and aspect. The path from the spatial to the temporal is well worn.

Reanalysis is a key mechanism of grammaticalization. A construction is reinterpreted by listeners as having a different structure than it had for previous speakers, even though the surface string is unchanged. The covert change in analysis can then surface in new patterns of use, and the construction has shifted.

Once a word has grammaticalized, the language may recruit a fresh lexical item to fill the function the old one has abandoned. The cycle, in which lexical material is repeatedly drawn into grammar and worn down, keeps a language continually renewing its stock of grammatical markers. Grammaticalization is thus a perennial source of new morphology.

Grammaticalization links synchronic variation to diachronic change. The range of uses a marker shows at one moment, from more lexical to more grammatical, often mirrors the historical stages it passed through. Reading the synchronic spread as a frozen record of the diachronic pathway is a standard inferential move.

The phoneme is an abstraction, not a sound that can be directly recorded. It is a mental category under which a speaker files a set of physically distinct sounds. What the microphone captures are the concrete realizations; the phoneme is the unit the grammar manipulates.

A single phoneme is realized by different allophones in different contexts. The variants are predictable from their phonetic surroundings, and a native speaker treats them as the same sound despite their physical differences. The phoneme is the equivalence class, and the allophones are its members.

Speakers are largely unaware of allophonic variation in their own language. They hear the contextually conditioned variants as identical, because perception is filtered through the phonemic categories of the native system. The abstraction is so deeply ingrained that the underlying physical differences become inaudible.

The same physical sound can belong to different phonemes in different languages, and a single phoneme in one language can split across two in another. Phonemic identity is therefore not a property of the sound itself but of the system in which the sound participates. The phoneme is relational.

The reality of the phoneme is supported by speakers' behavior. They group sounds, judge sameness and difference, and design writing systems around phonemic units. The convergent evidence from these behaviors is what justifies positing an abstract category rather than treating speech as a stream of unanalyzed sounds.

An archiphoneme is posited where a contrast that holds elsewhere is neutralized. In the position of neutralization the opposition between two phonemes is suspended, and the segment that appears belongs to neither one fully. The archiphoneme names this underspecified unit, abstracting away from the suspended contrast.

The phoneme mediates between the lexicon and pronunciation. A word is stored as a string of phonemes, and rules convert that abstract string into the detailed phonetic output. Without the intermediate phonemic level, the relationship between stored form and spoken form would have to be stated word by word.

Phonemic analysis seeks the smallest set of contrastive units that can account for all the meaningful distinctions in a language. The analyst pares away predictable variation, keeping only what is unpredictable and contrastive. The resulting inventory is a theory of which differences the language treats as significant.

The phoneme has been understood differently in different theoretical traditions, as a mental unit, a distributional class, or a bundle of distinctive features. Each conception captures part of what the term is meant to do. The disagreements show that the phoneme is a theoretical construct whose exact nature remains under discussion.

Whether the phoneme is a primitive unit or itself derivative has long been debated. Feature-based approaches treat the phoneme as merely a convenient label for a co-occurring set of features, with the features doing the real grammatical work. On this view the phoneme is a useful abbreviation rather than a fundamental object.

A relative clause modifies a noun by attributing a property to it through an embedded clause. The noun being modified is the head, and the relative clause is understood as a clause in which the head plays some grammatical role. The construction lets a whole proposition serve as a modifier.

Within the relative clause, the head corresponds to a position called the relativized position. The head may correspond to the subject of the relative clause, to its object, to an oblique, or even to a possessor. Languages differ in which of these positions they allow to be relativized.

The accessibility hierarchy ranks grammatical positions by how readily they can be relativized. Subjects are the most accessible, followed by objects, then obliques, with possessors and other positions less accessible still. A language that relativizes a lower position on the hierarchy generally relativizes all the higher ones too.

Relative clauses can be marked by a relative pronoun, by an invariant particle, by a gap alone, or by a resumptive pronoun left in the relativized position. The strategy a language uses can vary with the position being relativized, with lower positions more likely to require a resumptive pronoun.

A restrictive relative clause narrows down the reference of the head, picking out a subset of the things the head noun could denote. A non-restrictive relative clause instead adds a parenthetical comment about an already identified referent. The two types differ in intonation, in punctuation, and in their semantic contribution.

Relative clauses can be prenominal, following nominal, or internally headed. A prenominal relative precedes the noun it modifies, a postnominal one follows it, and an internally headed relative contains the head noun inside the clause itself. The position correlates broadly with the language's basic word order.

Subordination is the embedding of one clause within another so that the embedded clause functions as a constituent of the larger one. A subordinate clause may serve as a subject, an object, a modifier, or an adverbial. Subordination, unlike coordination, builds a hierarchical relationship rather than a relationship between equals.

Complement clauses are subordinate clauses that serve as arguments of a verb. A verb of saying or thinking takes a clause as its object, the embedded proposition being what is said or thought. The matrix verb determines what kind of complement clause it permits and how that clause is introduced.

Adverbial clauses are subordinate clauses that function like adverbs, specifying time, cause, condition, concession, or purpose. They attach to the main clause and situate the event it describes within a wider circumstantial frame. The subordinating conjunction signals which adverbial relation the clause expresses.

Languages vary in how heavily they rely on subordination. Some pack information into deeply embedded clauses, while others prefer to chain clauses together in looser, more coordinate fashion. The degree of clausal embedding a language favors is a structural and stylistic variable studied across discourse types.

subtopic: the McGurk effect and speech perception
sentence: Speech perception is not a simple matter of decoding an acoustic signal. The listener actively interprets a stream of sound that is highly variable, overlapping, and context-dependent. Recovering discrete linguistic units from this continuous and noisy input is a computational feat the perceptual system performs effortlessly.

subtopic: the McGurk effect and speech perception
sentence: The McGurk effect demonstrates that speech perception integrates information from more than one sense. When a listener hears one syllable while watching a face articulate a different one, the perceived syllable is often a blend of the two. The visible articulation alters what the listener consciously hears.

subtopic: the McGurk effect and speech perception
sentence: The McGurk effect shows that vision is not a mere supplement to audition in speech perception but is fused with it at an early stage. The listener cannot easily suppress the visual influence even when aware of the mismatch. The integration is automatic, suggesting a perceptual system built to combine the two streams.

subtopic: the McGurk effect and speech perception
sentence: The lack of invariance is a central puzzle of speech perception. The same phoneme is realized by very different acoustic patterns depending on the surrounding sounds, the speaker, and the rate of speech. There is no single acoustic template for a phoneme, yet listeners recognize it reliably across all this variation.

subtopic: the McGurk effect and speech perception
sentence: Categorical perception is the finding that listeners hear speech sounds in discrete categories rather than as points on a continuum. Along an acoustic continuum between two phonemes, perception flips sharply from one category to the other, and within-category differences are hard to detect. The continuous signal is partitioned into discrete units.

subtopic: the McGurk effect and speech perception
sentence: Coarticulation means that the articulation of one sound overlaps with that of its neighbors. The signal for a given segment is smeared across adjacent segments, so that information about one sound is carried by the acoustics of another. Listeners exploit this overlap, anticipating sounds from cues in their neighbors.

subtopic: the McGurk effect and speech perception
sentence: Phonemic restoration shows how strongly perception is shaped by expectation. When a speech sound is replaced by a noise, listeners often report hearing the missing sound clearly, the brain supplying it from context. The perceptual experience includes content that is not present in the signal at all.

subtopic: the McGurk effect and speech perception
sentence: Listeners normalize for the speaker, adjusting their interpretation of the signal to the voice they are hearing. The same acoustic pattern can be a different vowel depending on the speaker's vocal tract, and the perceptual system rapidly calibrates to each talker. Recognition is relative to an inferred speaker, not absolute.

subtopic: the McGurk effect and speech perception
sentence: Speech is perceived against a backdrop of lexical and contextual knowledge. An ambiguous stretch of signal is resolved toward a real word rather than a non-word, and toward a contextually plausible interpretation. Top-down knowledge and bottom-up signal are combined, so perception is an inference and not a passive reception.

subtopic: the McGurk effect and speech perception
sentence: Infants begin life able to discriminate the speech sounds of many languages and gradually narrow their sensitivity to the contrasts of the language around them. By the end of the first year, perception has been retuned to the native system, and discriminating non-native contrasts becomes harder. Experience reshapes the perceptual machinery.

Writing systems differ in the linguistic unit each symbol represents. An alphabet maps symbols onto individual consonants and vowels, a syllabary maps them onto whole syllables, and a logographic system maps them onto morphemes or words. The choice of unit shapes how the script relates to the spoken language it records.

An abjad is a writing system that represents consonants but leaves most vowels unwritten. Readers supply the vowels from their knowledge of the language and the context, recovering full words from a consonantal skeleton. The system works because the consonants carry the bulk of the lexical information in the languages that use it.

An abugida pairs each consonant symbol with an inherent vowel, and other vowels are indicated by systematic modifications of the consonant sign. The basic unit is a consonant with a default vowel, and diacritics or alterations change that vowel. The system sits between an alphabet and a syllabary.

Orthographic depth measures how directly a spelling system reflects pronunciation. A shallow orthography has a near one-to-one correspondence between letters and sounds, while a deep orthography is full of irregularities and historical residue. English orthography is notoriously deep, with many spellings preserving older pronunciations.

A deep orthography can encode morphological information that a purely phonetic spelling would obscure. Keeping a morpheme spelled consistently even when its pronunciation varies helps the reader recognize that the same unit recurs. The spelling sacrifices phonetic transparency to preserve a stable visual identity for each morpheme.

Logographic systems associate symbols with meaningful units rather than with sounds. A single character stands for a morpheme, and learning the system requires memorizing a large inventory of characters. Such systems are not tied to a particular pronunciation, which lets them be read across dialects that pronounce the same morpheme differently.

Writing is a comparatively recent and culturally transmitted technology, unlike spoken language, which every normal child acquires without instruction. A script must be deliberately taught and learned, and many languages have never been written at all. Writing is a tool layered onto language, not a part of its biological endowment.

Spelling reform is difficult even when an orthography is widely agreed to be inefficient. An established spelling carries the weight of literacy, tradition, and the inertia of printed material. Proposals to regularize a deep orthography repeatedly founder on the cost of changing what millions of readers already know.

The direction of writing varies across systems, running left to right, right to left, top to bottom, or in older scripts alternating direction from line to line. Direction is a conventional property of a script, not a necessity of the language. A single language can in principle be written in more than one direction if more than one script is used for it.

Punctuation and word spacing are part of an orthography but are not direct representations of speech sounds. They mark structure, grouping, and prosody, and many writing systems historically managed without spaces between words. The conventions for segmenting and pointing a text are themselves a learned and changeable part of literacy.

Information structure concerns how the content of a sentence is packaged for the listener, marking some parts as already known and others as newly contributed. The same proposition can be packaged in different ways, and the packaging guides the listener in updating a shared model of the discourse.

The topic of a sentence is what the sentence is about, the entity around which the rest of the clause is organized. The comment is what is said about that topic. Many languages have dedicated grammatical means for marking the topic, distinguishing it from the predication made of it.

Focus marks the part of a sentence that carries the most salient new information. In a reply to a question, the focus is the element that answers the question, the piece the listener did not already have. Languages mark focus through stress, through word order, or through dedicated particles and constructions.

The given-new distinction tracks what the speaker assumes the listener already knows against what is being added. Given information is treated as recoverable from the prior discourse or the situation, while new information is presented as not yet shared. Grammatical and prosodic choices align with this distinction.

Contrastive focus singles out one element against a set of alternatives, signaling that the chosen value is correct and the others are not. It does more than mark information as new; it explicitly rejects competing possibilities. Contrastive focus is often realized with especially prominent stress.

Some languages have a grammatical subject and a grammatically marked topic that need not coincide. A topic-prominent language organizes the clause around the topic, which may be distinct from the argument that controls agreement. The contrast with subject-prominent languages is a major typological division.

Word order is a primary resource for information structure. Fronting an element can mark it as a topic or as a contrastive focus, and the position of new information is constrained in many languages. The freedom to rearrange constituents is often in the service of packaging rather than of changing truth conditions.

Cleft constructions split a clause to put one element in a structurally focused position. The clefted element is presented as the answer to an implicit question, and the rest of the clause is presupposed. Clefts are a grammatical device for managing focus when intonation alone would be insufficient.

Prosody encodes information structure even when the syntax does not change. The placement of the main pitch accent in a sentence signals which element is in focus, and deaccenting an element marks it as given. The same string of words can convey different information structures purely through its intonation.

Information structure interacts with definiteness and pronominalization. Given referents tend to be expressed with reduced forms, such as pronouns, while new referents are introduced with fuller descriptions. The amount of linguistic material devoted to a referent tracks how accessible it is assumed to be.

A language is endangered when it is no longer being learned by children as a first language. Once intergenerational transmission breaks, the language is left with only adult speakers, and its future is finite. The number of speakers matters less than whether the youngest generation is acquiring it.

Language shift is the process by which a community gradually abandons one language in favor of another. The shift typically proceeds across generations, with the older language confined to ever fewer domains until it is no longer used at all. The community ends up monolingual in the language it has shifted to.

Endangerment is usually driven by social and economic pressures rather than by anything internal to the language. A language associated with mobility, employment, or schooling draws speakers away from a less prestigious local language. The shift is a response to the perceived advantages of the dominant language.

The vitality of a language can be assessed along several dimensions, including the absolute number of speakers, the proportion of the community that speaks it, the domains in which it is used, and whether it is being passed to children. Transmission to the next generation is the single most decisive factor.

Domain loss precedes outright language death. The endangered language is squeezed out of public and formal domains first, surviving longest in the home and in intimate settings. When even the home shifts to the dominant language, the last reservoir of transmission is gone.

A moribund language has speakers but no longer has children learning it. It is functionally a generation away from silence, since when the current speakers pass, no replacements will follow. Moribund languages are the most urgent targets of documentation, because the window to record them is closing.

Language documentation aims to create a lasting record of an endangered language before it falls silent. Recordings of natural speech, a description of the grammar, a dictionary, and a body of texts together preserve the language for scholarship and for any future community effort. Documentation does not by itself keep a language alive but it ensures it is not wholly lost.

Language revitalization attempts to reverse a shift by rebuilding the community of speakers. Strategies include immersion schooling, pairing fluent elders with younger learners, and creating new domains of use. Reviving transmission to children is the hardest and most essential goal of such efforts.

The death of a language entails the loss of a distinct system for categorizing and expressing experience. With it can go bodies of oral tradition, ecological and cultural knowledge encoded in its vocabulary, and a piece of the evidence about the range of possible human languages. Each loss narrows the record linguistics works from.

A language can also fall dormant, ceasing to have speakers while surviving in records, and later be reclaimed. Reclamation from documentation is difficult and depends heavily on the quality of the surviving material. The possibility of revival makes thorough documentation valuable even when a language has no current speakers.

Anaphora is the relationship between an expression and an earlier one that supplies its interpretation. A pronoun depends for its meaning on an antecedent, the expression it refers back to. Resolving anaphora means determining which antecedent a given pronoun is linked to.

Reflexive pronouns are anaphors that must find their antecedent within a restricted local domain, typically the same clause. A reflexive cannot be interpreted as referring to something far away in the discourse; its antecedent must be close. The locality requirement is a structural condition on reflexive interpretation.

Ordinary personal pronouns behave in a way that complements the reflexives. A personal pronoun must not take an antecedent within the same local domain, the very domain in which a reflexive must find one. The two kinds of element thus partition the space of possible antecedents between them.

Binding theory is the body of principles that constrains which expressions can corefer. It distinguishes anaphors, which must be bound locally, from pronominals, which must be free locally, from referential expressions, which must be free everywhere. The principles state structural conditions, not merely tendencies of interpretation.

Coreference is not the same as binding. Two expressions corefer when they happen to denote the same individual, but binding is a structural relation in which one expression is in a particular configuration relative to the other. Binding implies a structural dependency, while accidental coreference does not.

C-command is the structural relation that binding theory builds on. An element c-commands another, roughly, when it sits high enough in the tree to take the other within its scope. A binder must c-command the element it binds, so binding is sensitive to hierarchical structure rather than to linear order.

A bound-variable interpretation arises when a pronoun covaries with a quantified antecedent. When a pronoun is bound by a phrase such as every student, it does not pick out a fixed individual but ranges along with the quantifier. This reading is available only when the structural conditions on binding are met.

Reciprocal expressions, like reflexives, are anaphors subject to locality. A reciprocal requires a plural antecedent within the local domain and expresses a relation holding mutually among its members. Its distribution patterns largely with that of the reflexive, which is why the two are grouped together as anaphors.

Cataphora is the mirror image of ordinary anaphora, in which the pronoun precedes the expression that supplies its interpretation. A pronoun at the start of a sentence can be understood by a fuller noun phrase that comes later. The possibility of forward reference shows that anaphoric dependency is not strictly tied to linear precedence.

Anaphora resolution in discourse goes beyond the structural constraints of binding. When a pronoun has several grammatically possible antecedents, factors such as topicality, recency, and plausibility steer the listener toward one of them. Binding theory says which antecedents are permitted; discourse factors say which is preferred.

The hypothesis associated with Sapir and Whorf proposes that the language a person speaks shapes the way that person thinks. On this view, the categories a language imposes on experience are not neutral labels but influence perception and cognition. The structure of the language leaves a mark on the mind.

A strong form of the hypothesis, linguistic determinism, holds that language rigidly constrains thought, so that what cannot be expressed cannot be conceived. This strong form is now generally rejected, since speakers can entertain concepts their language does not encode and can borrow or coin words for new ideas.

A weaker form, linguistic relativity, holds that language influences thought without strictly determining it. Habitual patterns of expression make some distinctions easier to attend to and others easier to overlook. The weaker claim is empirical and testable, and it is the version most current research engages with.

Color vocabulary has been a central testing ground for linguistic relativity. Languages divide the color spectrum into different numbers of named categories, and researchers ask whether speakers of such languages also perceive or remember colors differently. The findings are mixed and have been interpreted in support of both relativist and universalist positions.

Studies of spatial language have asked whether languages that use absolute directions, like cardinal terms, for everyday description train their speakers to keep constant track of orientation. Speakers of such languages do appear to maintain a heightened sense of compass direction. The case is among the more persuasive evidence for a linguistic influence on cognition.

Grammatical categories, not only vocabulary, have been studied for relativistic effects. Whether a language obligatorily marks the gender of nouns, the shape of objects, or the source of evidence may direct habitual attention. The argument is that what a grammar forces speakers to specify becomes what they routinely notice.

A persistent methodological difficulty in testing the hypothesis is separating the effect of language from the effect of culture. Speakers of a given language usually share a culture, so a cognitive difference could stem from either. Careful designs try to hold culture constant while varying language, or to find the same language across cultures.

The hypothesis raises the question of whether the influence of language on thought operates only when language is actively used, as in remembering or describing, or whether it reshapes perception itself. Effects that appear in verbally mediated tasks but vanish in non-verbal ones suggest a thinking-for-speaking influence rather than a deep restructuring of cognition.

Whorf's own work focused on how grammatical patterns might encode an implicit metaphysics, a habitual way of construing time, substance, and events. His specific claims about particular languages have been heavily criticized and revised. The general idea that grammar carries habitual construals, however, continues to inform research.

Contemporary work tends to frame the question quantitatively, asking how much and under what conditions language influences cognition rather than whether it does so absolutely. The debate has moved from the sweeping early formulations toward measured claims about specific domains, specific tasks, and specific linguistic features.

Word formation is the study of how new words are built from existing material. The lexicon is not a fixed list but a system with productive processes for coining new items. Speakers can create and understand words they have never met, provided those words are assembled by the regular processes the language allows.

Derivation builds a new word by adding an affix that changes the meaning or the grammatical category of a base. Adding a suffix can turn a verb into a noun or an adjective into a noun, producing a related but distinct lexical item. Derivation contrasts with inflection, which produces grammatical variants of the same word.

Compounding combines two or more existing words into a single new one. The compound has a meaning that is related to its parts but is often more specific or idiosyncratic than their sum. One element typically functions as the head, supplying the basic category and the core of the meaning.

Conversion, also called zero derivation, creates a new word by shifting an existing one to a new category without any change of form. A noun used as a verb, or a verb used as a noun, exemplifies conversion. The relationship is derivational even though no affix marks it.

Blending fuses parts of two words into one, typically the beginning of the first and the end of the second. The resulting blend carries a meaning drawn from both sources. Unlike a regular compound, a blend usually clips its components rather than combining them whole.

Clipping shortens a longer word without changing its meaning or category. A multi-syllable word is reduced to one or two syllables, and the clipped form may eventually displace the original in everyday use. Clipping is a process of formal reduction rather than semantic derivation.

Acronyms and initialisms form a word from the initial letters of a phrase. An acronym is pronounced as an ordinary word, while an initialism is spelled out letter by letter. Both compress a longer expression into a compact form, and an acronym can become so familiar that its origin is forgotten.

Back-formation creates a new word by removing what is mistakenly analyzed as an affix from an existing word. A noun may be reinterpreted as if it contained a derivational suffix, and a corresponding verb is then formed by stripping that supposed suffix. The new word arises from a reanalysis of an older one.

Productivity measures how freely a word formation process can be applied to make new words. A highly productive affix attaches readily to new bases, including recent coinages and borrowings, while an unproductive one survives only in a fixed set of established words. Productivity is a matter of degree and can change over time.

Word formation processes interact, and a single word can be the product of several. A compound can be formed and then converted, or a clipped form can serve as the base for derivation. The lexicon is layered, with words bearing the accumulated traces of the processes that built them.

A sentence containing more than one quantifier can be ambiguous because the quantifiers can be understood in different relative scopes. A sentence saying that every child read some book can mean that each child read a possibly different book, or that there was one particular book that all the children read. The words are the same; the readings differ.

Scope describes which quantifier is interpreted as semantically wider than the other. A quantifier with wide scope is evaluated first, and the other is evaluated within its range. Switching which quantifier takes wide scope yields the two distinct readings of a scopally ambiguous sentence.

Surface scope is the reading in which the quantifiers are interpreted in the order they appear, the leftmost taking widest scope. Inverse scope is the reading in which the order of interpretation is the reverse of the surface order. The availability of inverse scope is a much-studied property of quantifier interpretation.

Scope ambiguity is not a matter of vagueness or of one word having two meanings. The individual words are unambiguous, and the ambiguity lies in how they are combined. This makes scope ambiguity a structural phenomenon, located in the semantic composition rather than in the lexicon.

Negation interacts with quantifiers to produce scope contrasts. A sentence with negation and a quantifier can be read with the negation scoping over the quantifier or the quantifier scoping over the negation. The two readings differ truth-conditionally, and which one a sentence allows depends on the construction.

Some semantic frameworks derive inverse scope by a covert movement that raises a quantifier above another at a level of representation distinct from the pronounced string. The quantifier is interpreted in its raised position even though it is pronounced in place. The covert operation reconciles the audible order with the inverted interpretation.

Not every pair of quantifiers yields a genuine ambiguity. Some quantifiers resist taking inverse scope, and some combinations have readings that are logically equivalent so that the ambiguity is not detectable. Which quantifiers can invert over which others is a fine-grained empirical question.

Scope is not confined to quantifiers proper. Modal expressions, negation, and certain adverbs also enter into scope relations, and a clause with several such operators can have multiple interpretations. The general phenomenon is the relative ordering of semantic operators in the composition of meaning.

The interpretation a hearer assigns to a scopally ambiguous sentence is influenced by plausibility and context, even though both readings are grammatically available. A reading that describes a sensible situation is favored over one that describes an odd one. Grammar furnishes the options; context biases the choice.

Quantifier scope offers a window onto the architecture connecting syntax and semantics. A single syntactic structure supporting more than one interpretation shows that meaning is not read off the surface string in a simple way. Accounting for the available and unavailable readings is a standard test of a theory of the syntax-semantics interface.

subtopic: the wave model and dialect continua
sentence: The wave model pictures linguistic innovations as spreading outward from a point of origin like ripples on the surface of water. A change starts somewhere and diffuses across the surrounding territory, weakening as it travels. Varieties closer to the origin adopt the change; those farther away may never receive it.

subtopic: the wave model and dialect continua
sentence: The wave model was proposed as a corrective to the family tree, which depicts language history as a series of clean splits. The tree cannot easily represent the fact that separated varieties go on influencing one another. The wave model captures this continued, gradient diffusion that the tree leaves out.

subtopic: the wave model and dialect continua
sentence: On the wave model, the boundary of any one innovation is just the limit of how far that particular ripple reached. Different innovations have different origins and different ranges, so their boundaries do not coincide. The result is a landscape of overlapping waves rather than a set of discrete branches.

subtopic: the wave model and dialect continua
sentence: A dialect continuum is the spatial pattern the wave model predicts. Adjacent local varieties differ only slightly and remain mutually intelligible, while the cumulative differences across many steps make the endpoints mutually unintelligible. Nowhere along the chain is there a sharp linguistic break.

subtopic: the wave model and dialect continua
sentence: In a true dialect continuum, the question of how many distinct languages are present has no purely linguistic answer. Any line drawn through the continuum is partly arbitrary, since intelligibility shades off gradually. Where one language is said to end and another begin is usually settled by political and social rather than linguistic criteria.

subtopic: the wave model and dialect continua
sentence: The wave model and the tree model are not mutually exclusive but capture different aspects of language history. The tree records the major splits caused by populations separating, while the wave records the diffusion of features across varieties that remain in contact. A full history needs both pictures.

subtopic: the wave model and dialect continua
sentence: An innovation that spreads as a wave can cut across the branches of a family tree. Two varieties belonging to different subgroups may share a feature simply because a wave of change passed over both. Such cross-cutting features are exactly what makes pure tree classification difficult.

subtopic: the wave model and dialect continua
sentence: Within a dialect continuum, the speed and reach of a wave depend on the density and direction of contact among communities. Barriers to interaction, whether geographic or social, slow or stop a wave. The shape of a feature's distribution thus records the historical pattern of who talked with whom.

subtopic: the wave model and dialect continua
sentence: A focal area is a region from which innovations repeatedly radiate, while a relic area is one that successive waves failed to reach. Mapping focal and relic areas reconstructs the historical dynamics of a continuum, showing where change originated and where older forms were sheltered.

subtopic: the wave model and dialect continua
sentence: Modern variationist work refines the wave picture by tracking how innovations spread through populations as well as across space. A change can move from one social group to another and from one urban center to another, sometimes leaping over the intervening countryside. The diffusion has a social geometry as well as a physical one.

Most speech sounds are produced on a pulmonic egressive airstream, with air pushed out of the lungs by the respiratory muscles. This is the default mechanism, and a language can build its entire sound inventory on it alone. Other airstream mechanisms exist, but the pulmonic egressive one is universal.

Ejective consonants are made with a glottalic egressive airstream. The closed glottis is raised, compressing the air trapped above it, and the consonant is released with a characteristic sharp burst. No lung air is involved in the release, which distinguishes ejectives from ordinary pulmonic stops.

Implosive consonants use a glottalic ingressive airstream. The glottis is lowered while loosely vibrating, drawing air inward, so that the consonant is released with an inrush rather than an outrush. Implosives are voiced and have a distinctive hollow quality produced by this downward glottal movement.

Clicks are produced with a velaric ingressive airstream, independent of the lungs and even of the glottis. A pocket of air is rarefied between two closures in the mouth, and releasing the front closure produces the click sound. Because the mechanism is oral, a click can be made while breathing or even while phonating other sounds.

Nasalization results from lowering the soft palate so that air flows out through the nasal cavity. For a nasal consonant the oral tract is fully blocked and all the air escapes through the nose. For a nasalized vowel the oral tract stays open and the air escapes through both passages at once.

Nasal consonants and nasalized vowels both involve an open velum, but they differ in whether the oral cavity is also open. The velum is the gate, and its position determines the nasal or oral routing. A language can contrast oral and nasal vowels by the position of this gate alone.

Nasalization spreads readily between segments. A vowel next to a nasal consonant tends to pick up nasal airflow from it, often as a predictable allophonic effect. In some languages this contextual nasalization has been phonologized, so that nasal vowels become contrastive in their own right.

The velum can be lowered to varying degrees, so nasalization is not strictly all-or-nothing in the physical signal. Phonological systems nonetheless treat it as a discrete property, classifying segments as nasal or oral. The categorical phonological feature abstracts away from the gradient physical reality.

The choice of airstream mechanism is one of the dimensions that distinguishes consonants. A full articulatory description specifies not only place and manner and voicing but also which airstream initiation produces the sound. Sounds made on rarer airstreams are unevenly distributed among the world's languages.

Different airstream mechanisms can be combined within a single language and even cued in quick succession. A speaker of a language with both pulmonic and glottalic consonants switches the initiating mechanism from segment to segment. The vocal apparatus thus operates several distinct airflow systems that the grammar can recruit.

Typology classifies languages by their structural properties and searches for patterns in how those properties are distributed. Rather than studying one language in depth, typology surveys many languages to discover what kinds of systems occur and what kinds are rare or absent. The aim is to chart the space of possible human languages.

An absolute universal is a property claimed to hold of every human language without exception. The claim that all languages have vowels and consonants, or that all distinguish nouns from verbs, would be of this kind. Absolute universals describe the necessary skeleton shared by all languages.

A statistical universal is a strong tendency rather than an exceptionless law. Most languages may show a particular trait while a few do not, and the universal records the strong skew without claiming it is absolute. Much of typology deals in such tendencies, since exceptionless universals are comparatively few.

An implicational universal links two properties, stating that the presence of one implies the presence of another. If a language has property A it will also have property B, though a language can have B without A. Implicational universals constrain which combinations of features can co-occur.

Word order universals are a classic domain of implicational typology. The order of verb and object correlates with the order of other pairs, such as adposition and noun or noun and genitive. A language tends to be consistently head-initial or head-final, and the correlations hold across the pairs.

Markedness is a typological notion ranking the members of a category by how basic or how special they are. The unmarked member is the default, more frequent across languages and within texts, while the marked member is the special case. Implicational universals often state that having the marked member implies having the unmarked one.

Typological generalizations call for explanation, and several kinds are offered. A pattern may reflect a constraint built into the language faculty, a pressure from how language is processed, a tendency of how grammars change over time, or a bias in how speech is perceived and produced. Typology supplies the facts that such explanations must account for.

Building a reliable typological sample is itself a methodological challenge. Languages are not statistically independent, since related languages share traits by inheritance and neighboring ones by contact. A sample that overrepresents one family or area can manufacture a spurious universal, so samples are designed to be balanced.

Rarity is informative in typology. A structural type attested in only a handful of languages, or in none, raises the question of why it is dispreferred. The gaps in the attested space are as much a part of the data as the common patterns, since both must follow from whatever shapes possible languages.

Typology connects synchronic distribution to diachronic process. A common type may be common because many independent paths of language change converge on it, and a rare type rare because few paths lead there. The frequency of a structure across languages can thus be read as a trace of the dynamics of change.

Vowel harmony is a phonological pattern in which the vowels of a word are required to agree in some feature. The vowels within a single word are not chosen independently; they must share a value for the harmonic property. A word that mixed vowels of opposite values would be ill-formed.

In a backness harmony system, all the vowels of a word must be front or all must be back. A suffix added to a stem takes whichever value the stem's vowels carry, so the suffix has a front and a back variant. Which variant surfaces is determined by the word it joins.

Rounding harmony requires the vowels of a word to agree in lip rounding. A suffix vowel becomes rounded after a rounded stem vowel and unrounded after an unrounded one. The harmony makes the rounding of a suffix predictable from the stem rather than fixed in the suffix itself.

Vowel harmony makes affixes alternate systematically, so a single suffix appears in two or more shapes. The shapes are not separate morphemes but contextual variants of one, selected to harmonize with the stem. The morphology must be stated in terms of an underlying form plus the harmony process.

Some vowels are transparent to harmony, neither triggering it nor blocking it. The harmonic feature seems to pass straight through a transparent vowel as if it were not there, so the vowels on either side of it still agree. Transparent vowels are a classic puzzle for theories of how harmony propagates.

Other vowels are opaque, blocking the spread of harmony and imposing their own value on what follows. An opaque vowel acts as a barrier, so the word is divided into stretches with different harmonic values. The contrast between transparent and opaque vowels constrains models of the process.

Vowel harmony is often analyzed as the spreading of a feature across the word from a trigger. The feature, originating in the stem, extends rightward or leftward and associates with each eligible vowel it reaches. The spreading account treats harmony as the same kind of operation as local assimilation, scaled up to the word.

Harmony systems differ in how strictly they apply. Some require harmony throughout the native vocabulary but allow disharmonic loanwords, and some have exceptional stems that resist harmonizing their suffixes. The exceptions show that harmony is a rule of the grammar that can have a limited and specifiable domain.

Vowel harmony lends a word a kind of phonological cohesion, since the shared feature unifies all its vowels. The pattern can help a listener tell where one word ends and the next begins, because a switch in the harmonic value signals a likely word boundary. Harmony thus has a parsing function as well as a structural one.

Harmony is not limited to vowels. Some languages have consonant harmony, in which consonants within a word agree in a feature such as place or secondary articulation. The parallel shows that long-distance agreement among segments is a general possibility, and vowel harmony is its most widespread instance.

subtopic: the poverty of the stimulus argument
sentence: The poverty of the stimulus argument claims that the linguistic input a child receives is too sparse and too degenerate to account for the rich grammatical knowledge the child ends up with. The conclusion drawn is that some of that knowledge must be supplied in advance, as part of the child's innate endowment.

subtopic: the poverty of the stimulus argument
sentence: The argument turns on a gap between input and attainment. Children acquire grammatical generalizations that go far beyond the sentences they have actually heard, and they avoid errors that the input gives them no direct way of ruling out. Something must bridge the gap, and the proposal is an innate component.

subtopic: the poverty of the stimulus argument
sentence: A key part of the argument concerns negative evidence. Children are rarely and unreliably corrected for ungrammatical utterances, yet they come to know that certain sentences are impossible. Without systematic information about what is not allowed, the child's knowledge of impossible structures needs another source.

subtopic: the poverty of the stimulus argument
sentence: Certain structures are claimed to be acquired correctly even though the input contains few or no examples that would distinguish the correct grammar from a plausible wrong one. If both grammars fit the data the child hears, the child's reliable convergence on the right one cannot be driven by the data alone.

subtopic: the poverty of the stimulus argument
sentence: The standard response within a nativist framework is to posit a universal grammar, a set of principles and constraints common to all languages and available to the learner before any experience. The learner's task is then narrowed to fixing the options that distinguish particular languages, a far more tractable problem.

subtopic: the poverty of the stimulus argument
sentence: Critics of the argument question its empirical premises, asking whether the input is really as impoverished as claimed. Large corpora of child-directed speech are examined to see whether the relevant examples are genuinely absent. If the data do contain the needed evidence, the argument loses its force.

subtopic: the poverty of the stimulus argument
sentence: Another line of response grants that the input underdetermines the grammar but argues that general-purpose learning mechanisms can still succeed. If the learner is equipped with statistical and inductive biases that are not specific to language, these biases plus the data may be enough. The dispute then concerns the nature of the prior, not its existence.

subtopic: the poverty of the stimulus argument
sentence: The poverty of the stimulus argument is sometimes formulated as a logical problem and sometimes as an empirical one. As a logical problem it concerns what any learner could in principle infer from a given kind of data. As an empirical problem it concerns what children actually hear and what they actually learn.

subtopic: the poverty of the stimulus argument
sentence: The argument has been central to the debate between nativist and empiricist views of language acquisition. Both sides agree the child brings something to the task; they disagree about how much, how specific, and how language-particular that contribution is. The poverty of the stimulus argument is where that disagreement is joined.

subtopic: the poverty of the stimulus argument
sentence: Modeling work tests the argument by building computational learners and measuring what they can acquire from realistic input. A learner that converges on the target grammar from child-like data, using only general biases, weakens the case for language-specific innate knowledge. The argument is thus increasingly evaluated by simulation.

Politeness is a dimension of language use concerned with managing the social relationship between speaker and hearer. The same message can be conveyed more or less politely, and the choice signals respect, distance, or solidarity. Politeness is studied as a systematic part of how language works in social interaction.

An influential framework analyzes politeness in terms of face, the public self-image that participants in an interaction seek to maintain. Negative face is the desire not to be imposed upon, and positive face is the desire to be approved of. Many polite strategies are ways of attending to one or both kinds of face.

Negative politeness strategies minimize an imposition on the hearer. They include hedging a request, apologizing for the intrusion, and giving the hearer an easy way to decline. Such strategies show deference and respect the hearer's freedom from imposition.

Positive politeness strategies appeal to the hearer's desire to be liked and included. They include expressing approval, claiming common ground, and using markers of in-group solidarity. Where negative politeness keeps a respectful distance, positive politeness narrows it.

Honorifics are grammatical and lexical resources dedicated to encoding respect. Some languages have honorific pronouns, honorific verb forms, and special vocabulary used when speaking to or about a respected person. The honorific system grammaticalizes social relations that other languages handle through optional strategies.

Honorific systems can register several distinct relationships at once. A single verb form may simultaneously mark deference toward the addressee, deference toward a referent, and the formality of the setting. The choice of form is a continuous social calculation rendered in the morphology.

The T-V distinction is a widespread, more modest form of honorific marking, a contrast between a familiar and a respectful second-person pronoun. The choice between the two pronouns encodes the speaker's reading of the relationship, and a switch from one to the other can itself be a social act.

Politeness is not the same as indirectness, though the two often coincide. An indirect request can be a way of being polite, but directness is appropriate and even expected in some relationships and situations. What counts as polite is calibrated to the context rather than fixed by the linguistic form.

Norms of politeness vary across communities, and a strategy that is polite in one may seem cold or intrusive in another. The relative weighting of imposition, social distance, and relative power differs from culture to culture. Politeness research therefore studies both the general framework and its local realizations.

Politeness phenomena reveal that the choice of linguistic form is sensitive to social structure. Power, distance, and the seriousness of an imposition all feed into how an utterance is framed. The grammar and lexicon supply the options, and the social configuration of the moment selects among them.

The principle of compositionality holds that the meaning of a complex expression is determined by the meanings of its parts and the way they are combined. Knowing the words and the syntactic structure should, in principle, be enough to compute the meaning of the whole. The principle explains how finite knowledge yields infinitely many meanings.

Compositionality is what allows speakers to understand sentences they have never encountered. A novel sentence is interpreted by combining familiar word meanings according to familiar rules of composition. Without compositionality, every sentence would have to be learned individually, which is plainly impossible.

On a compositional account, the syntactic structure of a sentence guides its semantic interpretation. The way the words are bracketed into constituents determines the order in which their meanings are combined. A change in structure, even with the same words, can therefore change the meaning.

Idioms appear to challenge compositionality, since the meaning of an idiom is not predictable from its parts. An expression like kick the bucket does not mean what its words separately suggest. Idioms must be stored as units, which is why they are treated as a partial exception to the compositional principle.

Even apparently non-compositional expressions are usually only partly so. Many idioms allow some internal variation and inflection, suggesting they are not entirely frozen. The relationship between the storage of idioms and the general compositional machinery is a delicate matter for semantic theory.

Compositionality is naturally paired with a recursive syntax. Because syntactic rules can apply repeatedly to build ever larger structures, the composition of meaning can apply repeatedly in step. The unboundedness of the sentences a language can form is matched by the unboundedness of the meanings it can express.

Context-dependence raises questions for a strict reading of compositionality. The contribution a word makes can shift with the context, and pragmatic enrichment can add content beyond what the words encode. Semantic theories accommodate this either by enriching the inputs to composition or by adding a pragmatic layer after it.

Compositionality is best understood as a constraint on the relation between syntax and semantics rather than as an obvious empirical fact. It says that the meaning function must be definable in terms of the parts and the mode of combination. Whether a given phenomenon respects the constraint is often the substantive question.

The principle of compositionality underlies formal approaches to meaning, in which each syntactic rule is paired with a semantic rule that says how to combine the meanings of the daughters. Building meaning rule by rule alongside structure makes the interpretation of a complex expression a calculable result.

Quantifiers, modifiers, and operators all test the compositional machinery, because their contribution depends on what they combine with and in what order. Working out how the meaning of such an expression is assembled from its parts is much of the daily business of formal semantics.

When a word is borrowed from one language into another, it is rarely taken over unchanged. The borrowing language reshapes it to fit its own sound system, a process called loanword adaptation or nativization. The adapted form may differ noticeably from the source, having been remade in the image of the borrower's phonology.

Loanword adaptation reveals the phonotactic constraints of the borrowing language by showing how it repairs forbidden structures. A consonant cluster the language disallows is broken up, and a syllable shape it does not permit is reshaped. The repairs are systematic, exposing the rules that govern native words.

A foreign sound absent from the borrowing language is typically replaced by the nearest available native sound. The substitution is consistent, so the same foreign sound is mapped to the same native one across many borrowings. The pattern of substitutions is a map of how the borrower's inventory relates to the source's.

Vowel epenthesis is a common adaptation strategy. To break up a cluster or to repair an illicit coda, the borrowing language inserts a vowel, and the choice of which vowel to insert is itself rule-governed. The inserted vowel is often a default that the language uses for this purpose generally.

Loanwords are often adjusted to carry stress and tone according to the borrowing language's patterns. A borrowed word receives stress in the position the native system would assign it, and in a tone language it is fitted with tones. The prosodic adaptation integrates the word fully into the receiving system.

Loanwords may also be reanalyzed morphologically, with part of the foreign word reinterpreted as an affix or with native affixes attached to make it inflect. Once a loanword takes native inflection and derivation, it behaves like any other word and can spawn further forms. Morphological integration completes the nativization.

There is debate over whether loanword adaptation is computed over the source's sounds or over the source's spelling and over how much the adapter's perception of the foreign form drives the result. Adaptations sometimes reflect what the borrowers heard, sometimes what they read, and sometimes a compromise.

The degree of adaptation can vary with the social standing of the source language and the bilingualism of the borrowers. Highly bilingual speakers may keep loanwords closer to the source, while monolingual speakers nativize them more thoroughly. The same word can thus exist in more and less adapted variants.

Older loanwords tend to be more thoroughly nativized than recent ones, having had longer to be assimilated. A language's vocabulary can therefore contain layers of loans at different stages of adaptation. The least adapted forms are usually the most recent arrivals.

Loanword adaptation is valued by phonologists as a natural experiment. The borrowing language is presented with structures it would never generate on its own and must repair them. Watching how it does so tests theories of the language's phonology against data the native lexicon could never supply.

Sentence parsing is the process by which a listener or reader builds a syntactic structure for an incoming string of words. Parsing happens incrementally, word by word, as the sentence unfolds. The parser cannot wait for the end; it commits to an analysis as it goes.

A garden path sentence is one that leads the parser into an initial analysis that later turns out to be wrong. Partway through, the reader is forced to abandon the structure built so far and reanalyze. The momentary breakdown and recovery is what makes such sentences feel jarring.

Garden path effects show that parsing is incremental and that the parser makes commitments before it has all the information. If the parser waited until the end of the sentence, no garden path could occur. The very existence of the effect is evidence about how parsing operates in real time.

When several analyses are momentarily available, the parser tends to favor one over the others. One proposal is that it prefers the structure with the fewest nodes, attaching new material in the simplest way. The garden path arises when this preferred structure is the one the sentence does not ultimately support.

Another proposed parsing preference attaches an incoming phrase to the most recently built constituent. This locality bias usually serves the parser well but occasionally leads it astray. When the correct attachment is to a more distant constituent, a garden path or at least a processing slowdown can result.

Not all temporary ambiguities cause noticeable garden paths. Whether the reader is led astray depends on which analysis the parser prefers and on how strongly the context and the plausibility of the words bias the interpretation. A temporary ambiguity that resolves toward the preferred reading passes unnoticed.

Lexical and semantic information can steer parsing away from a garden path. The likelihood that a particular verb takes a particular kind of complement, and the plausibility of a noun as an agent or a patient, feed into the parser's choices. Parsing draws on more than bare syntactic structure.

Reanalysis, the revision of an abandoned structure, is not always easy or even possible. Some garden path sentences are so severe that readers cannot recover the correct parse without conscious effort. The difficulty of reanalysis is itself a measure of how committed the parser had become.

Garden path sentences are a tool for studying the human parser experimentally. By measuring how reading slows at the point of disruption, researchers infer what analysis the parser had adopted and when it noticed the conflict. The sentences are designed to make the parser's hidden choices observable.

The study of parsing distinguishes the grammar, the speaker's knowledge of what structures are possible, from the parser, the mechanism that applies that knowledge in real time. A garden path sentence is perfectly grammatical; the difficulty lies entirely in processing it. Competence and performance come apart in exactly such cases.

subtopic: the comparative method and sound laws
sentence: A sound law is a statement of a regular sound change, specifying that a particular sound shifted into another under stated conditions throughout the history of a language. The law is exceptionless within its domain: every word meeting its conditions underwent the change. Sound laws are the regularities that historical phonology discovers.

subtopic: the comparative method and sound laws
sentence: The claim that sound change is regular was a methodological breakthrough. Once changes are assumed exceptionless, apparent counterexamples become informative, since each must be explained by borrowing, by analogy, or by a further sound law. The regularity hypothesis converts messy data into a solvable puzzle.

subtopic: the comparative method and sound laws
sentence: A famous early success in formulating sound laws described a systematic shift of the stop consonants in one branch of Indo-European. The shift applied across the board, and its regularity made the relationship of that branch to the rest of the family demonstrable. The law became a model for the whole enterprise.

subtopic: the comparative method and sound laws
sentence: An apparent exception to a sound law can be resolved by discovering a further conditioning factor. A residue of words that seemed to violate one law was later shown to obey it perfectly once the position of an original accent was taken into account. The exception was not random; it pointed to a missing condition.

subtopic: the comparative method and sound laws
sentence: Analogy is the great disturber of regular sound change. While a sound law operates blindly on phonetic shape, analogy reshapes a form to match a related form in its grammatical paradigm. The two forces pull in different directions, and the messy surface of a language is the outcome of their competition.

subtopic: the comparative method and sound laws
