sentence: Sound laws are chained in a relative chronology. One change must have happened before another if its output became the input to the second, and the ordering of the laws can be reconstructed even without dates. The relative chronology is part of what the comparative method recovers.

subtopic: the comparative method and sound laws
sentence: Sound laws are formulated by inspecting the regular correspondences among cognate words in related languages. A correspondence that recurs systematically is the reflex of a single change, and stating that change as a law accounts for the whole set of cognates at once. The law is the explanation of the correspondence.

subtopic: the comparative method and sound laws
sentence: The conditioning environment of a sound law specifies exactly where the change applied: before certain sounds, in certain syllable positions, under certain accentual conditions. A change that looks irregular may simply have a more complex conditioning environment than first supposed. Refining the environment is how exceptions are absorbed.

subtopic: the comparative method and sound laws
sentence: Borrowed words can violate a sound law because they entered the language after the change had ceased to operate. A loanword that fails to show an expected reflex is therefore suspect as a borrowing, and its irregularity becomes a clue to its origin. The sound law turns into a diagnostic for distinguishing inherited from borrowed material.

subtopic: the comparative method and sound laws
sentence: The cumulative discovery of sound laws lets the historical linguist reconstruct the phonology of an unattested ancestor and the sequence of changes leading to each descendant. The proto-language and the laws together constitute a model of a family's history. Testing the model is a matter of checking that the laws derive the attested forms.

A clitic is an element that is grammatically a separate word but phonologically dependent, unable to stand on its own and attaching to a neighboring word as a host. Clitics occupy an awkward middle ground between full words and affixes, and identifying them tests the very notion of the word.

A proclitic leans on the word that follows it, and an enclitic leans on the word that precedes it. The clitic forms a single phonological unit with its host even though the two are syntactically distinct. The direction of attachment is a property of the particular clitic.

Clitics differ from affixes in their host selectivity. An affix attaches to a base of a specific category, but a clitic can typically attach to whatever word happens to occupy the relevant position, regardless of its category. The promiscuity of host choice is a diagnostic that separates clitics from affixes.

Clitics often appear in a fixed position in the clause rather than next to the word they are semantically associated with. A clitic may be required to come second in its clause, attaching to whatever word lands in first position. Such positional clitics show that the clitic's placement is governed by the clause, not by its host.

A clitic cluster forms when several clitics line up together in a fixed order. The order within the cluster is rigidly specified by the grammar and need not reflect the syntactic relations of the elements. The cluster behaves as an ordered template that the clitics must fit into.

Distinguishing a clitic from an affix on one side and from a full word on the other relies on a battery of criteria. These include whether the element can be separated from its host, whether it can be stressed, whether it shows host selectivity, and whether it can be coordinated. No single test is decisive; the criteria are weighed together.

The word is a less straightforward unit than everyday intuition suggests, and clitics are a prime reason. A phonological word, defined by stress and by phonological rules, need not coincide with a grammatical word, defined by syntactic distribution. A clitic and its host are one phonological word but two grammatical words.

Special clitics have a distribution different from that of the corresponding full word, while simple clitics are merely reduced, unstressed variants that occupy the same positions as their full counterparts. The distinction separates clitics that are syntactically special from those that are just phonologically weak.

Clitics are a frequent waypoint in grammaticalization. A full word may first become a clitic, leaning on a host, and later become a full affix, fused to it. Watching an element move along this cline, the historical linguist sees the boundary between word and affix being crossed in slow motion.

Pronouns are especially prone to cliticization, since they are frequent, short, and often unstressed. Many languages have a full set of stressed pronouns and a parallel set of clitic pronouns, used in different positions. The clitic pronouns may eventually become agreement affixes on the verb, completing a well-trodden path.

A consonant cluster is a sequence of two or more consonants with no vowel between them. Languages vary widely in which clusters they permit, ranging from systems that allow none at all to systems that tolerate long strings of consonants. The set of permitted clusters is a core part of a language's phonotactics.

Sonority is a scale ranking sounds by their inherent loudness or openness, from the least sonorous stops up through fricatives, nasals, and liquids to the most sonorous vowels. The scale is invoked to explain why some sound sequences are favored and others avoided. Sonority gives the syllable its characteristic shape.

The sonority sequencing principle states that, within a syllable, sonority should rise from the onset toward the nucleus and fall from the nucleus toward the coda. A cluster that respects this rising-then-falling profile is well-formed, and one that violates it is cross-linguistically rare or repaired.

An onset cluster typically arranges its consonants so that sonority increases toward the vowel. A cluster of a stop followed by a liquid obeys this pattern, since the liquid is more sonorous and sits closer to the nucleus. A cluster that put the more sonorous consonant first would run against the principle.

Some clusters are systematic exceptions to sonority sequencing. A sequence of a fricative followed by a stop at the start of a word violates the rising-sonority requirement, since the fricative is more sonorous than the stop. Such sequences are common enough that they are often given a special status outside the ordinary syllable.

The sonority distance between adjacent consonants in a cluster matters as well as their order. Languages may require a minimum gap on the sonority scale, permitting a cluster only when its members are sufficiently far apart. A small sonority distance can make an otherwise well-ordered cluster ill-formed.

Languages with restrictive phonotactics repair illicit clusters rather than tolerating them. A vowel may be inserted to break a cluster apart, or a consonant may be deleted to eliminate it. The repairs surface most visibly in loanwords, where the borrowing language is confronted with clusters its grammar forbids.

Coda clusters tend to be more restricted than onset clusters in many languages. The end of the syllable allows fewer combinations, and where a coda cluster is permitted its sonority should fall toward the syllable edge. The asymmetry between onset and coda is a recurrent typological observation.

The syllabification of a string of consonants between two vowels depends on which clusters the language allows as onsets. A medial cluster is divided so that as many consonants as possible begin the following syllable, provided the result is a legal onset. Sonority sequencing constrains where the division can fall.

Sonority is also implicated in which consonants can function as syllable nuclei. When a language allows a syllabic consonant, it is almost always one of the more sonorous consonants, a nasal or a liquid, rather than a stop. The pattern follows from the close link between sonority and the ability to carry a syllable.
